speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):

speechtext:
The answer to both questions is "no", but I know that this is a matter of interest to the hon. member and several other hon. members who have been asking similar questions, and perhaps to supplement the answer I might read the last letter I wrote in that connection to the premier of Saskatchewan, and which will show why a decision is being deferred at the moment. The letter is dated June 11, 1955, and reads:
Thank you for informing me in your letter of June 8 of the steps the Saskatchewan government is taking to repair the damage caused by this spring's rains and floods in your province.
I appreciate your desire to have an early decision on the degree of federal assistance, if any. I wish to assure you that one will be made just as soon as the federal government is confident that it has all the available information upon which to make its decision, not only with respect to your province but also with respect to Manitoba. As you no doubt have read in the press, the Manitoba government has announced that it too will be seeking assistance from the federal government and is presently collecting data upon which to base its claim for aid.
As the damage in both provinces was due to similar factors, I am confident that you will appreciate why, in the interests of equality of treatment, we would prefer not to make any decision until we have also received Manitoba's request. In the meantime we are giving earnest consideration to the representations that have been made by Saskatchewan.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman saw in the press, as I did this morning, that the premier of Manitoba declared that he had not yet received all the details that he felt were required to submit his request.

Mr. Speaker, I rise really for the purpose of asking for information. I notice that this is an amendment to the Criminal Code. My request for information is based largely on the fact that I have not the bill in question. I am not sure whether the bill has been

circulated. If not, I suggest that second reading be deferred until members have the bill before them.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext:
I now have the bill. Perhaps I could make my point. Then the minister may be able to satisfy me on the question that I wish to raise.
As I understand the status of parimutuel systems, for some years past the federal government has not been levying a tax on parimutuel bets, having vacated that field of taxation to the provinces some time after the 1945-46 dominion-provincial conferences. My recollection is that only the provincial governments are now levying any imposts on bets which are made in the parimutuel betting system at racing meets. If that is so and if the federal government is entirely out of that field as a taxation field, I raise the question of whether it is desirable for the federal government again to become involved, -for whatever purpose it may be-in what in effect would be a tax on the proceeds of parimutuel betting and thereby to re-establish the duplication of taxation in this field which existed during the war.
There is probably a serious question of jurisdiction involved as well as the difficulty of double taxation. I understand that the purpose is to provide funds for the policing of betting, more particularly in rural racing meets. But surely the policing of race meets is an obligation of the law-enforcement officers and the police under the Criminal Code; and surely that is something which falls or should fall on the general fund of the country and is not something for which the government should attempt to recoup itself by entering into a field of taxation which it has already abandoned in favour of the provinces.
I raise this point for information largely because I have not had the opportunity to see the bill. I am not sure what its full import is. If the purpose is as it appears to be, namely a means of raising some revenue for policing purposes, it is an odd thing that it should be done through the Criminal Code in any event. Perhaps I might let the matter rest there until more information is before the house.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as to the question that has been raised, it is true that during wartime we had what was to all intents and purposes a tax on parimutuel betting. I think it was 2 per cent. That money came into the treasury of Canada directly. The present proposal does not interfere in any way with the right of the provinces to take a certain proportion of the amount wagered at each race meet. In some of the provinces the amount is as high as 12 per cent. This measure does not interfere in any way whatsoever with that right. The amount of one-half of one per cent is taken off all wagers apart altogether from what the provinces do and does not restrict in any way their rights to impose whatever tax is provided now.
The half of one per cent is simply to finance certain things which are already being done but to finance them in a slightly different manner. Previously we have charged large or small fairs and race meetings of any size so much a day for each mounted policeman or civilian who went there to supervise. The average up to now has been $27. The average under the new plan will be about $40 a day. A small race association may only have retained an amount totalling $70 to $80 a day, and if we have to send two officials to do the job it will require more money than the total intake of the race meeting. At the present time supervision is not being carried out at many of these places because they just go ahead and conduct races without supervision. That is not very satisfactory. Under the law we would probably have to prosecute in such cases or someone, most likely the province, would have to prosecute.
Therefore it is thought to be advisable to make sufficient money available in order to see to it that whatever supervision is necessary will be provided. If one man can do the job, all well and good. If we have to send two, then two will be sent, but there will be no interference with the intake at any particular race meet. My friend calls it a tax. We call it a fee charged all race meetings that take place in the country. It is the amount necessary to pay for the supervision whether at large or small race meetings.
Criminal Code

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.
On clause 1-Operation of parimutuel system.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext:
I think that this is the most unusual piece of legislation, under the guise of criminal law, that has ever been brought before this house. I wonder if that is one of the reasons why the Minister of Justice himself is not piloting this legislation through the house. To me this represents a situation that should not find its place in any criminal code of this country. I am referring particularly to subsection 3 and the words additional thereto.
In the explanatory notes it states:
The purpose of the amendment is to permit an additional combination of heat races and dashes.
To that there can be no objection. However, subsection 3 now provides:
No parimutuel system of betting shall be used upon any race course unless the system has been approved by and its operation is carried on under the supervision of an officer appointed by the Minister of Agriculture,-
No\v, that has been the system in the past. However, this very indirect subsection is brought into being. The amendment reads:
and the person or association conducting a race meeting shall pay to the Receiver General of Canada one-half of one per cent of the total amount of bets, made through the agency of a parimutuel system operated under such supervision, on any race run at such meeting.
This appears to me like a subterfuge whereby an offence is created under the Criminal Code in anticipation. The parimutuel is operated and there is no offence in the operation of a parimutuel which is subject to supervision at the moment. However, this does not provide that a person is exempted from responsibility under certain circumstances. It makes it an offence for any association conducting a race meeting not to pay to the Receiver General of Canada one-half of 1 per cent.
If it were intended to be an exculpatory section, it would read something like this: No parimutuel system of betting shall be used unless the system has been approved by-and I am not objecting to the words there-an officer appointed by the Minister of Agriculture, and unless the person or association conducting the race meeting pays to the Receiver General of Canada one-half of 1 per cent of the total amount of bets.
This is the most strangely drafted piece of legislation. I believe it is the first amendment to the Criminal Code since the new Criminal Code came into effect. In my opinion this is an indirect method of the

Criminal Code
Receiver General of Canada enforcing the collection of money, and making it an offence for failure to pay money. Supposing they did not pay it, what happens? They conduct a parimutuel operation this year at a fair and they do not pay the amount to the receiver general. How long have they got within which to pay it? When is the offence created? Supposing the fair does not pay it for six months or eight months? Is the offence created after the date the receiver general finally decides he wants the money? In other words, when does the statute of limitation start to run? It does not say it shall be forthwith, and it does not say how long after the race it shall be paid, the day of the race or a week after the race? When does the offence begin?
I object to this section on two grounds. One, it is the first time that, under the Criminal Code, an offence has been created for the failure to pay money, because unless there is an offence under this section it is a meaningless addition to the Criminal Code, if it were to be an exculpatory provision' unless the person or association conducting the race meeting pays to the Receiver General of Canada one-half of one per cent on the day of the race, a week after the race or a day provided for.
These two objections should be given consideration, because surely we are not going to make it an offence under the Criminal Code to fail to pay taxation. This is the first time it has ever been tried. It has meritorious possibilities, because if the Minister of National Revenue wants to make it an offence under the Criminal Code punishable by a jail sentence on failure to pay income tax it can be done. He has never tried that. This is the first time under the Criminal Code, as far as I have been able to examine it, that an offence punishable with a maximum fine of $500 under the summary conviction sections or six months in jail for the failure to pay a tax levied by the receiver general has been tried The receiver general is to have made available to him one-half of one per cent of the total amounts of the bets. I suggest that some further consideration should be given to this matter and that certainly parliament should not be asked to provide for the thin edge of the wedge so that from now on this can be taken as an example from which the revenue authorities may make it an offence punishable with a fine and jail sentence for failure to pay taxation.
I presume it was never intended that this section should have that result; but in the wording, in the form and in the general 
set-up it provides for imprisonment for failure to pay a debt, either a fine under the summary convictions provisions or in default of the payment, fine or imprisonment.
I should like to hear from the attorney general, the Minister of Justice, on this matter because it is a singular circumstance that the Minister of Agriculture is piloting through the house this novel piece of legislation which cannot be justified in any way unless parliament is to be asked to make it an offence punishable by a fine and imprisonment for failure to pay a debt.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, before the Minister of Justice speaks on the matter I might only say that for the 20 years I have been here there never has been any doubt so far as the minister bringing in the bill and piloting it through the house is concerned. There has been amending legislation brought in on at least half a dozen, maybe a dozen occasions. I have not checked them all, but there has been legislation dealing with these very sections on many occasions in the last 20 years, and long before that-I do not know how far back these sections have been under agriculture-but this particular item has always been under the Minister of Agriculture in my time, and it so states in the code.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext: Administration.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext:
Unless this house changes it, it is under the Department of Agriculture. The original reason for putting it under the Department of Agriculture is that agriculturists are concerned with the promotion of the breeding of light horses, including standard bred horses, running horses and all other kinds of horses. This has always been considered a part of the exhibitions that are put on for the purpose of encouraging agricultural production; that is, small fairs or big fairs or any other kind of meet of that nature. Therefore, agriculture has had something to do with it.
If it was the proper thing in those earlier days, it is still more necessary now. The kind of horse that is most necessary on a farm today in this northern country is a light horse. Out in our part of the country where you are not able to get to town in the wintertime from most of the farming areas without horses it is not a heavy horse you want, it is a light horse. Therefore, the department is more interested today in promoting the breeding of light horses than it ever was before.
We were very much interested in promoting the breeding of draft horses at one time, but today it is mostly light horses. For

that reason it has always been under the administration of the Department of Agriculture.
I am not a lawyer and my hon. friend is. Of course, so is the Minister of Justice. But I still think I can read the English language and understand it. I think the suggestion made by my hon. friend would result in the claim that it was the intention to make something criminal much stronger than the way it is worded. Although I had very little to do with drafting the bill, yet I did state what we wanted put in it. As a result of that I presume some good draftsman drafted it and it is worded as it is. It says:
No parimutuel system of betting shall be used upon any race course unless the system has been approved by and its operation is carried on under the supervision of an officer appointed by the Minister of Agriculture, whose duty it shall be to stop the betting before each race and to see that no further amounts are deposited,-
That is the wording as it was and as it is. There is added:
-and the person or association conducting a race meeting shall pay to the Receiver General of Canada one-half of one per cent of the total amount of bets, made through the agency of a parimutuel system operated under such supervision, on any race run at such meeting.
All the provinces have provisions which provide payments must be made to them. The provision in Quebec is for 51 per cent; Prince Edward Island, 5 per cent; Ontario, 7 per cent; Manitoba, 10 per cent; Saskatchewan, 5 per cent; Alberta, 5 per cent; British Columbia, 12 per cent. These amounts are set up. With respect to the enforcement of them, I do not know that there has ever been any enforcement necessary. The payments are made automatically as a result of whatever the funds are that come in and so far as I know there has never been any necessity to prosecute anybody. I do not see how there would be in this case.
This is something which the associations themselves want to do. They desire to have it done this way so that there will be supervision of all fairs, and similar supervision of all race meets where there is parimutuel betting. You will not have one kind of supervision at one and another kind at another, and when it gets to be so small it is impossible to have that kind of supervision they have all suggested this means of meeting the situation, and not have people appealing to them all the time to see that this or that fellow is prosecuted but to have the thing operated without prosecutions. That being the case, I doubt very much whether there would be any prosecution in any case in spite of the fact the Criminal Code says there are certain penalties if you do not carry out all the terms of the code. The suggestion really
Criminal Code
is that instead of this being stated in the Criminal Code we pass other legislation. I assume the reason for this being in the Criminal Code is that there are some kinds of betting that are considered to be illegal. This kind of betting under these circumstances is made to be legal. It is not a matter of making a criminal out of someone; it is a matter of trying to operate in a manner that will be satisfactory without making people criminals.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext:
Perhaps I might now supplement the information which I think is necessary to a proper view of this bill. As I understand the amendment, it requires the payment of one-half of one per cent of the total amounts of bets at every race course using the parimutuel system, which of course involves the whole of Canada, and I should think some very substantial sums of money. Can the minister give the total amount that is bet under the parimutuel system in the course of a year? My recollection is that it would run to perhaps $200 million or more. While one half of one per cent may seem a small amount, actually it might mean a levy of from $10 to $12 million. That is much greater than the amount which the Department of Agriculture is endeavouring to recoup because of the administrative costs of supervising betting at the smaller fairs.
Apparently the department has been charging smaller fairs the cost of two inspectors at $35 per day each, or a total of $70 a day. I do not think anyone will agree that there should be a continuance of a levy of that sort on the smaller fairs because it makes it impossible for them to provide the same facilities as are enjoyed by the larger places.
I am not quarrelling with the objective of the minister, that is, to remove from the smaller rural fairs the proportionately heavy cost of supervision which is necessary in order to make legal the parimutuel betting system, but that could be accomplished in other ways. That is a problem for the Department of Agriculture.
As my colleague has indicated, we have here an amendment to the Criminal Code which I agree, as has been suggested, is an entirely improper way to raise funds, even though there is a direct association of ideas because this matter has been under the Department of Agriculture before. As a matter of fact the Minister of Finance is involved here as this is really a second budget. The Minister of Agriculture is bringing down a budget today in which he wants $10 million or $12 million, and that should be added to the budget we have already had.

Criminal Code
I should correct my figure, it is perhaps $1 million or $2 million, but in any event it is a sizeable sum in any budget, whether brought in by the Minister of Finance or by one of his colleagues.
We should have the exact amount before us. As I said, I agree with the suggestion which has been made that this matter might well be reconsidered, for two reasons. First, because of the way in which it is being done. It is not proper to have it in the Criminal Code. Second, because of the objection I made originally that we have here a return of the federal taxing authority into the parimutuel field which was abandoned in 1947 so that the provinces could enjoy that field of taxation themselves.
It is all part of the agreements and the fiscal relationships between the two levels of government. The provinces count on obtaining a certain amount of money from this field and now we have the federal government returning to a competitive position in that field.
Then I would raise briefly the question of jurisdiction. The Minister of Agriculture has indicated that all provinces are concerned with the supervision of fairs and they all take a levy from the parimutuel betting. Is it necessary to have two governments in this field of supervision of the parimutuel betting system? I suggest that it is not necessary and that the whole matter might be reviewed with a view to making arrangements under which the government which taxes the parimutuel betting-that is, the provincial government-should also have responsibility for the supervision. However, that is a matter of procedure.
As I say, I am not quarrelling with the objective of seeing that the parimutuel systems where they are operated legally are operated fairly and in the interests of those who enjoy that sort of pastime. Of course that involves supervision, and it then becomes a question of how that should be done. I object seriously and strenuously to what has been called taxation through the Criminal Code.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is a point raised by this amendment which has not really been dealt with by the Minister of Agriculture and which it does seem he has not grasped. Under the section which now exists there is the exception to the ordinary prohibition on betting by the Criminal Code. There is a provision under which parimutuel betting shall be allowed where its operation is

carried on under the supervision of an officer appointed by the Minister of Agriculture. The existing section provides that that shall be at the expense of the operation. Whether we agree with this new method of dealing with things of this kind, the fact is that the exception that has been made provides that the cost of the operation be borne by the association.
This amendment introduces an entirely new principle. The Criminal Code says that, in spite of the prohibition on betting generally, parimutuels may be conducted in certain cases and under certain terms where there is an officer on hand to supervise the activities and that this officer shall be appointed by the Minister of Agriculture. Then the amendment goes on to say, and I quote from the amending clause:
The person or association conducting a race meeting shall pay to the Receiver General of Canada one-half of one per cent of the total amount of bets, made through the agency of a parimutuel system operated under such supervision, on any race run at such meeting.
That introduces two entirely different ideas. First of all, there is a provision that this payment shall be made. Then this immediately creates an offence under the section. The law is clear that where there is an offence created without a penalty accompanying it, there are certain general provisions that apply. The penalties in fine and otherwise are established. They would operate immediately in this case. So the possibility of fine, and other penalty in the event of the fine not being paid, is immediately established by this amendment. That is a new idea.

At the moment it is a declaration that this shall be done at the expense of the association. This is a provision that the money shall be paid to the Receiver General of Canada. The second point I wish to make is that this is a new idea. This is not a provision that the operation shall be carried on at the cost of the particular organization. It is a provision that a certain percentage be paid to the Receiver General of Canada. It is true that in the fantastic figures placed before us, to a minister who would say, "What's a million anyway?", $412,000 may appear almost insignificant; but the fact
Criminal Code
remains that there is a new idea that the Criminal Code is now becoming a taxing law. That has never been done before. There is no other provision in the Criminal Code that makes it a taxing law. This is a completely new principle and a very dangerous principle. Mark you, the one-half of one per cent does not approximate the present cost. The present cost is given as a figure in excess of $200,000, but this is simply taken out of the bag and one-half of one per cent is put in. If one-half of one per cent is justified, 10 per cent would be just as much justified. It would be simply for the government to decide what tax is going to be paid by the associations for the privilege of conducting activities of this kind.
The federal government was in the parimutuel tax before, but at the request of the provincial governments, which have the constitutional responsibility, it got out. Now it is getting back in again under another device, and this is making the Criminal Code a taxing law. There is no other section of any act in the Criminal Code that produces a corresponding situation. The remarks I am making are in no way directed against the provision of a method of this kind for supervision, but it would be just as logical to charge a particular tax for those who are doing this because some officer must be there as to say to a warehouse man, for instance, that because the warehouse near a dock requires special police protection, therefore a certain percentage of the cost of the operation of that warehouse shall be paid to the Receiver General of Canada. In fact, it would be just as reasonable to say that every one of us who does not like to be set upon on the public highways and otherwise requires protection by policemen shall pay to the Receiver General of Canada a certain percentage for that protection.
The Criminal Code at all times has been a code dealing with laws that protect the rights of the people of Canada. The enforcement of that in general is under the provinces. There are, of course, special circumstances where the federal government under some sections has a particular obligation. In general, however, through the fact that the exclusive jurisdiction over the administration of justice is under the provincial governments, they have the responsibility. In fact, we know that the supervision of race tracks is under the provincial governments, and at least one provincial government and perhaps more have set up racing commissions for the purpose of supervising these activities.
The responsibility of the federal government is to deal with the criminal law. It

Criminal Code
is the responsibility of the provincial governments to enforce these laws. In addition to the various penalties and exceptions that are created, this is a completely new idea. It makes the Criminal Code for the first time a taxing law. No matter how small the amount may be in the opinion of the government, that fact does not change the principle involved; and I should think the government would be well advised to drop this bill and let the matter stand where it is now or to provide some other method of facilitating the opportunity to small fairs to carry on a provision of this kind by creating penalties and exceptions which will be easily enforceable by the provincial authorities who have that responsibility.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, a little while ago I made a suggestion and I think the attorney general might give consideration to it. No one has any objection to the objective of having the matter of light horses and the connection with light horses remain with the Department of Agriculture. The objective is most laudable. The purposes in mind are desirable ones to be achieved. But it is not desirable that parliament turn itself into an institution which prescribes that the penalty for failure to pay a debt to the crown is a fine and imprisonment. Sending people to jail for failure to pay debts has been abolished. It used to be a novel and easy way of dealing with the matter. Certainly the present plan could be very well carried on until I think many of the difficulties of the Minister of Finance would be relieved. We just need to put in ano.ther "and" and make the provision read, "and unless income tax is paid on this amount" or any other type of tax. Whoever drafted this bill failed to realize what was in fact being done, however eminent that person was.
I want to point out again how, if the word "unless" were in this section, the entire situation would be changed. In other words this is supposed to be an exception. You are not going to operate betting unless certain things are done. You are not going to operate parimutuel machines unless certain things are done. As the law stands now, it says:
No parimutuel system of betting shall be used upon any race course unless the system has been approved . . .
And so on. That sentence ends with a semicolon and a new sentence begins:
. . . and the person or association conducting a race meeting shall pay to the Receiver General of Canada one-half of one per cent of the total amount of bets, made through the agency of a parimutuel system . . .

Surely it is perfectly clear that you are by that provision creating a disjunctive offence. You are making an offence the failure to pay the Receiver General without stating when the offence begins. When is the offence committed? Is it committed at the time the first bet is made, or the second bet or the last bet, or is it committed at the end of the year when the fair winds up its business? When does the offence begin? That is the reason I make this suggestion, and it removes the criticism that this legislation provides imprisonment for failure to pay taxes. This was meant to be an exception, and a desirable one. If my hon. friend would simply accept this suggestion-and I am not saying it is perfect; the matter of the exact wording will have to be considered-I think it would meet the objection. There can be a semicolon and then he can say:
. . . and unless the person or association conducting a race meeting pays to the receiver general one-half of one per cent of the total amount of bets made through the agency of a parimutuel system operated under such supervision or any race run at such race meeting directly after the conclusion of the race meeting
Then you create an offence which has a beginning. Then you remove from this section the dangerous import of the section which is that we have arrived at a point where, in order to achieve the laudable end of properly controlling race meetings, we are going to make failure to pay tax an offence punishable under the Criminal Code.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in what the
Minister of Justice has just said he has in no way dealt with the fact that this introduces a principle which has no parallel in the Criminal Code. His reference to section 178, subsection 6, only emphasizes the difference. It does not satisfactorily explain. What he has pointed out is that under subsection 6 of section 178 there is power to

Criminal Code
impose fines. Of course if such fines were imposed there would be the penalties that flow from the imposition of the fines if they were not paid. That happens all through the code. There is nothing new in that. There has been no place in the code at any time where the code has become a taxing act.
The Minister of Justice nods his assent to the proposition I have put forward. This measure declares for the first time that as the result of a certain provision in the code a tax-and it is nothing else-of a certain percentage of the take from the betting shall be paid to the Receiver General of Canada. I point out this is a new principle. I suggest it is an unsound principle. If you once accept the proposition that half of one per cent can be paid, then for the purposes of revenue there is no reason why at some future time it might not be 5 per cent, 10 per cent or any other figure. It is all very well to say that the half of one per cent is being imposed with some relationship to the anticipated cost. I think the Minister of Justice would be well advised not to support a measure of this kind, which he knows has no parallel, because if he does so he is starting a new concept of the code, that it is not merely a code of laws defining the things that shall not be done to injure society or individuals within society, subject to certain exceptions such as the one we have here, but that in addition there shall be a tax for the service rendered.
If there is to be a tax in this case for the service rendered, there is no reason why there should not be a specific tax for policing, a specific tax for our protection from certain dangers that are dealt with in the code, because unquestionably the setting up of many of these protective features in the act does involve public expenditure. Heretofore that public expenditure has always been part of the system of the administration of justice except in those special cases where federal authorities such as the Royal Canadian Mounted Police or others have taken their own special field of duties.
I urge the minister to consider carefully how dangerous and unwise it would be to open the door to a new type of disguised taxation, a system of taxation that at some time in the future might very conveniently become the device by which some other government at some other time could say: Well, here is a very easy way for us to raise additional moneys. I may say that within our ranks we have some who are known to be very strong advocates of the encouraging of the breeding of horses of this type. I know there are those within our ranks and doubtless on the other side who have a personal interest, as well as an interest based

on their public responsibility, in the proper organization of these races which have the effect of encouraging the breeding of light horses. We are in hearty agreement with that. We all want to see the small fairs encouraged so that they will be able to do the things that will help them finance their general activities as well as give local encouragement to horse breeding.
But let us not in the name of that encouragement, let us not simply because we all want to make it possible for the small fairs as well as the large racing organizations to have their fair opportunity, introduce a system of taxation which, once started, can expand upon itself and can then be extended to other sections of the act very readily if the principle can be regarded as sound in this particular case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am not anxious to protract the debate but there are one or two points I should like to make quite clear because I think it is most important that the position of the government should not be misunderstood in relation to them. I am sure that I can agree quite unequivocally and unreservedly with the Leader of the Opposition that the Criminal Code should not be a taxing statute. Were it not for the fact that the very group of sections with which we are dealing here providing for the carrying on of a parimutuel system throughout Canada are in themselves exceptional, I do not think there would be any desire to add this amendment to them. I think that those in Canada who have conscientious, strong views in opposition to gambling in any form, even parimutuel, would not take kindly to the idea that the general body of the taxpayers should have to pay money to supervise the operation of a parimutuel system.
That being so, the Leader of the Opposition's fear that the operation of this amendment is something which can be extended to raise money for the general revenue of the country is, I suggest, and I am sure upon reflection he would agree, that it is quite without foundation. The only way in which we could possibly justify, the only way in which we do justify this deduction of one-half of one per cent of the bets, is merely to defray the necessary costs of the supervision of these parimutuel race meetings. That being so, while I am in complete agreement with the Leader of the Opposition on the general principle, I think that the application of a little common sense to the matter with which we are specifically dealing at the moment indicates very clearly that we are trying to provide for the proper supervision of parimutuel betting throughout Canada by those

Canadians who see no harm in it and who like to place a bet. Throughout Canada we provide for such proper supervision, but we provide it properly at their expense. We make it quite clear in this amendment that we are not going to affront those who have strong feelings against gambling, by saying that they have to dig down in their pockets as taxpayers and put up part of the cost of running the parimutuel system of which they disapprove.

speechtext:
We have heard a lot about the legal aspects of this bill. I am somewhat like the Minister of National Revenue when it comes to the legal aspects of parliament. I am a babe in the woods, as I think he said he was. I should like to turn to some of the practical aspects of this bill.
In the first place, the Minister of Justice was talking about the supervision of parimutuel betting, and up until now I believe that has been a provincial responsibility. I can say to him that so far as parimutuels are concerned they are supervised by the provincial authorities, because I believe they get about 5 per cent from that source. Provincial officials are at every race meeting to look after their interest in that 5 per cent. In addition, the provincial police are always on hand.
I agree with the Minister of Agriculture that the harness horse needs some help in this country in filling the place it should occupy. On many, many of our farms today the draft horse is giving way to this type of horse, which is big enough to do farm work and also able to enter the light harness show class and run races. In order to make horse raising profitable, you have got to facilitate ways and means for horses to make some money as race horses. If the farmers of this country get well-bred stock, they can show these horses at the fairs as well as race them.
I should like to ask the minister if this amendment was requested by the small fairs. It seems to me that on the one hand you are taking this half of 1 per cent but you are not handing it over to the small fair. You add $40 or $80 per day as the cost of policing or supervising the racing, and you are doing nothing to help these people. You are taking your pound of flesh from that small fair. The minister knows that I have been to him many times seeking help for the small fairs in my riding. I know the same condition exists throughout the whole of Canada in so far as these small fairs are concerned. If, under the terms of this bill, the minister is going to take his pound of flesh, then he should put something in the bill that is going to help these class B and C fairs.
Criminal Code
When you come to the standard-bred horse association and the trotting association of Canada, you find that they are taken care of by qualified members and officers. I believe that this bill will result in a lot of duplication of services. How are you going to protect the collection of your half of 1 per cent? It is suggested the mounted police will be there to supervise some of these small fairs and the parimutuel betting. I believe that today the small fair cannot afford parimutuel betting because there is never enough money coming in. It has been tried many times at small race meetings and small fairs. I cannot see how this bill will help the small fair in that respect because when you come to taking care of all the officials it takes to run a parimutuel machine, you will find there will never be enough money taken in through the deduction of this half of 1 per cent to pay these officials. This bill will not help the small race meetings; it will just take the pound of flesh from them.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext: You have missed a lot of fun in your life.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext:
I know I have missed a lot of fun in different ways, but I just do not do it. I just want to say it is not a thing on which I am personally informed or able to instruct others.
The Criminal Code provides that certain kinds of betting are illegal, that certain things that are done are illegal in connection with wagering of any kind. Then it goes on to set up a system or indicate that if we are going to have this parimutuel betting, then it must be supervised to see that illegal things are not done. One of the illegal things that might be done is for the association to keep too much of the money that is paid in, and not allow those who are running the horses to get a sufficient proportion of the money that is bet. It is for that reason we set out in the code the provision that the association can take a proportion, that the provinces can take a proportion and so on.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext: May I ask the minister whether or not that is totally under the jurisdiction of the provinces in this country?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext: No, not when it comes to parimutuels.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext:
It is.

Criminal Code

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext:
No; if you are operating parimutuel betting and have supervision it must be by the Department of Agriculture for the dominion government. The reason this amendment is put forward is that the smaller fairs, as my hon. friend says, cannot afford parimutuel systems. They have just gone along without supervision, and we are asked to prosecute these associations. We say it is the responsibility of the province to prosecute. The buck is passed back and forth between the two and some people say, "Well, they are breaking the law, why are they not prosecuted?" The only reason I can find for their breaking the law is that, as my hon. friend has said, at these smaller places there is not enough money taken in to cover the entire costs. Therefore, the cost is not going to be charged up against the small fair and the small operators of race tracks who cannot afford to pay these costs. It is going to be charged against the whole wagering, and the result will be those wagering at the smaller fair will pay only a small proportion of it. Those wagering at the larger operations will pay the larger proportion. Their reason for being favourable to it, as they expressed it to us, is that they do not want racing to get into bad repute simply because those smaller places are not properly supervised and some people get the idea that parimutuel betting is carried on in larger places just the same as it might be in some places where it is not properly supervised. So they say, have them all properly supervised and take sufficient funds in order to see that they are. That is what we are attempting to do.
Under the present provisions of the Criminal Code the expenses incurred in carrying out the provisions of parimutuel betting at race meetings is borne by the racing associations, and they are assessed by means of a fixed rate per supervising officer detailed for each day of racing. We do that now. We put a supervising agent in there, and we have the authority to close the place up at the end of any race or before any race starts if the race is not being carried on in accordance with the regulations which the Minister of Justice referred to a moment ago when he said that our department has the authority to make regulations.
We go on to say that this rate of assessment, which was fixed at $27 per day under the system, required some $200,000 for the cost of administration. I think it was $257,000. The cost of administration was fixed at $27 per day for each supervising officer detailed for the 1953 and 1954 racing seasons. An increase to $40 is necessary to cover the total expenses of the department incurred in connection with race track supervision in
[Mr. Hodgson.j
1954, even though the various supervising details were already below the required strength and all operating costs were cut to a minimum. In carrying out the Criminal Code in its present state it will be necessary to raise the fixed rate of assessment to $40 per day for each supervising officer detailed to cover the entire cost, although even with this increase the department will still be compelled to operate below the desired strength and at restricted expenses, as in 1954. It was found that the $27 per day fixed rate was creating a hardship on the smaller racing associations, fairs and exhibitions, and the increase of this fixed rate to $40 per day will undoubtedly, if enforced, compel smaller associations to discontinue operations.
If the proposed amendment is enacted the greater proportion of the revenue derived from such a method of assessment would be forthcoming from the larger centres at no cost to any racing association. The anticipated increase in revenue would enable this department to carry out proper supervision to provide the necessary services at all racing meetings regardless of size and location.
To answer the question as asked, it simply means that the smaller association will pay only this 2 per cent of the entire amount which is wagered there, and which will be very much below what will be necessary to pay their costs of supervision.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext: Two per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext:
One-half of one per cent, rather. The old rate was 2 per cent during the war. One-half of one per cent of the total amount wagered, and the large associations will at the same time pay one-half of one per cent and the necessary funds to conduct proper supervision at the smaller places will be taken from the wagering at the larger operations. That money will be available through estimates of the department and used accordingly.
One thing that I cannot go along with was said by the Leader of the Opposition and also by the hon. member for Prince Albert, namely, that some new principle is being introduced into this. There is no new principle in this.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext: The Minister of Justice agrees.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext:
I do not agree with either of you, then, because the fact is that now we collect $40 from, say, Humboldt under the regulations as they are. We go there and collect $40. If they do not pay the $40 we will close them up. We have that right. If our regulations say they must pay $40, there is a $500 fine under this section if they are

not acting in accordance with the regulations. That is not changed at all. The fact of the matter is that we have practically removed the offence in so far as anybody is concerned who would be liable to anything of that kind. We said we are not going to inflict on you $40; we are not going to inflict a particular amount in that way. We are simply going to say that one-half of one per cent must be taken out of the amount wagered. Then there would be no offence committed by anyone. Now there is an offence if the $40 is not paid. If there is any change it is that there may be an offence now. With this amendment there will be none. The one-half of one per cent will not amount to anything like $40; therefore no new offence is being introduced, or no new element is being introduced into it.
I think that is fully borne out by what is stated in the section referred to by the Minister of Justice. Subsection 2 of section 235 of the old Criminal Code reads as follows:
. . . the Minister of Agriculture if he is not satisfied that a proper proportion of gate receipts and percentages taken from the parimutuel pools is being given in purses to horses taking part in the race meeting,-
And all these things affect it; the amount that you are taking out for this purpose, that purpose and the other purpose, affects the amount that goes to the persons taking part in the race meeting. The section continues: -or that the provisions of this section are not being carried out in good faith by the person or association conducting the race meeting, may at any time order the parimutuel machines to be locked and their operation stopped for such time as he may think fit.
That is done, of course, through those men who are there supervising. In most cases it is a mounted policeman who is sent there to supervise. We send him there and he checks every one of these activities following the races, or he has officials who are sent there under this provision and they report to the police if they are not carrying on as the regulations state. The police has the authority to close it down, to stop the betting. And, as is said in the section that we are proposing to amend, he can stop any race where provisions are not being made for the proper distribution of those funds. Therefore I cannot see that there is any change in principle between what is done now and what is to be done under this. We are simply making sure that at the end of the different races a certain amount of money has been wagered. It is a very simple matter to figure out what one-half of one per cent is of the amount that has come in, and that one-half of one per cent goes to the federal treasury.
The other 7 per cent, which is mentioned in the legislation with regard to Ontario, goes to 50433-3244
Criminal Code
Ontario. A certain amount goes to the association and all the rest of it must be divided among those who race the horses. It is protection of people who raise these horses. If anyone has any doubt that it is not important to have that kind of thing encouraged, may I say this. Every time I want to breed a mare on my farm in Saskatchewan I have to load her into a truck and take her at least 35 miles; that is, if I want to get a cross with a light horse. It is about 35 or 40 miles from my place to Lipton. The closest horse I can find in that part of the country is at Lipton; it is owned by a man who raises horses; and that is true all over the country. The men who are racing horses have these sires. You can take your mares to them and have them bred. That is the reason why the agricultural department is in it at all. We are interested in making certain that there are enough of these horses around to do the necessary breeding that must be done by farmers. Farmers cannot keep sires for light horses the same as someone who is interested in racing, and the result is that the farmers can take their mares there to breed. This act is intended to encourage the keeping of enough horses around the country to be used as sires in order to get the type of horse we want.
I cannot see that there is anything wrong in it. If there is any difference in principle between enforcing the collection of $10 and enforcing the collection of $40, I cannot see it. Now we are out to collect $40, let us say from Humboldt. On the basis of one half of one per cent of the amount that I read here a few moments ago, the total would be $886. One half of one per cent of that amount would be $4.43. We must enforce the collection of that smaller amount under the amendment, and before we had to enforce the collection of the $40. I cannot see that there is any new principle involved. I think the bill should go through as it is. It is not going to do any harm, either to the principles of taxation or to anything else.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext: I am glad the minister mentioned the fair at Humboldt as an example because I have been there on two or three occasions and I know something about it. If you imposed a fine of $500 I wonder whom you would get it from; and if you could not find someone to get it from, who would go to jail-the president or the secretary?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION

Not being a lawyer I hesitate to get entangled in this debate. I think there is a misunderstanding here. I agree entirely with the minister when he says that there is justification for trying to help the smaller racing associations. I know there will be

Criminal Code
advantage to the horse breeding associations and to horse breeders across this country. I realize that they are trying to help them out.
Our objection is not on that basis at all, our objection is simply to the fact that the Receiver General of Canada is going to have this one-half of one per cent of what is bet at these races. As the hon. member for Prince Albert and the Leader of the Opposition have mentioned, this is an innovation in connection with the Criminal Code which should not be a taxing statute.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION

I objected to doing that on the ground that if I brought such a provision into the house there would be a long debate on the matter. As it is, we collect $40 but we would not be allowed to collect a smaller amount. If I was wrong in that, that might be a way of correcting it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext: I am quite serious in saying that I think the minister was wrong in suggesting that the receiver general get this instead of the Department of Agriculture. speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext: If these collections came into the department I would have absolute control over the expenditure of that money. I could do anything that the department advised should be done, up to the total amount.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext: And you know of some of the things your department can do.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext: I have heard a lot of things said about that. I have an idea what would be said if I brought that into the house. As it is, the money will go to the receiver general and if I want any of it I will have to come to the house with an estimate.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext: The same thing would be true the other way. It would appear in the estimates of the minister's department and he would have to come to the house and state where that money had gone.

speechtext: Only if it comes in to the receiver general.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext: Would you not have to provide it by a vote?

speechtext:
In 1945 the dominion government returned this taxing field to the provinces and now they are going back into it by collecting one-half of one per cent of the amounts wagered. As the Leader of the Opposition just said, there is nothing to stop

them raising it to 5 per cent or 10 per cent. By a simple amendment to the act it can be changed to anything.
I suggest that the department should collect this money and retain it in a trust fund from which costs would be taken. If the surplus got too large, either you could eliminate the assessment for a few years until the fund got back to normal, or the percentage could be reduced to one-quarter of one per cent. That would eliminate all this trouble. I can understand why this is obnoxious to some hon. members in the house who realize that it is an innovation in connection with the Criminal Code. Surely the Minister of Justice would have something to say on this.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext: I do not think I can add anything to what I have said already. I think everything has been said that should be said and we might just as well settle it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext: Will any more officials be required to administer this, or will it be done by the mounted police?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext: We will not need any more officials. The supervision out in the country is done by the mounted police and unless it is necessary to have a plain-clothes man go some place to check up something, they would handle it. It is indicated here that the cost of supervision has been $27 a day, but with an indicated daily cost of $40 there may be some new help used.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext: You think that occasions of that kind will be few and far between?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my remarks at this time are directed chiefly to the Minister of Justice. This is one occasion when I think we can agree that what we are concerned with is the encouragement of the small fair or other meeting place where races of this kind are held. I think everyone will agree that any method of supervision of the particular exceptions to the Criminal Code in connection with the prohibition of betting and gambling should not discourage the operation of that exception in those smaller fairs where these races constitute an important part of the activities.
If there is one place where the breeding of light horses will be encouraged it is in the smaller places where these races are held. That is highly desirable, and it is also highly desirable that appreciation of the light horse and interest in the light horse be created by races of this kind. It is not only the breeding of the light horses that is important. The breeding of the light horses will be encouraged if the general public understands the value of the light horses. For that reason we all agree that anything that

is done to make it easier for the small fairs to operate within the exceptions provided by the Criminal Code should be done as long as it is consistent with the general application of the Criminal Code and the general enforcement. Now let us see what the Minister of Agriculture has really said. He has told us that this change will not involve the appointment of any additional staff.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext: I had not intended to say it will not require the appointment of any additional staff.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext:
At least the impression was given that it would certainly not involve the appointment of any substantial number. The minister was careful to point out that in the rural areas the enforcement in the ordinary course of events would be by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. We must remember that the argument that is being presented to us is in regard to those small places. Therefore on the basis of the minister's own argument the enforcement is going to fall mainly on the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police is a force maintained by the government for the general supervision of our laws and for carrying out police duties related to federal legislation. That being the case, I suggest to the Minister of Justice that in consultation with the Minister of Agriculture he consider the advisability of following an entirely different course than is suggested here.
It seems to me that the new amendment introducing for the very first time since confederation the principle of taxation under the Criminal Code is the outgrowth of something that perhaps never should have been done in the first instance. There were sections that prohibited gambling and betting and various activities, which would have prevented and did prevent the operation until these amendments were made in the first place of the parimutuel system of betting. Then under the section which it is now proposed to amend there was a provision that parimutuel betting could be carried on where it was authorized by the government and where there was a certain type of supervision. We are told that in the rural areas, where this is most important from the point of view of the present discussion, it will be done by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. It is not possible that the first mistake was the insertion in the sections of the provision that this should be done at the expense of the association? If this is to be done by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, why have it at the expense of the association at all? Why not let the Royal Canadian Mounted Police carry out these
Criminal Code
duties just as they carry out other duties in relation to other laws passed by the dominion government? Why would it not be just as well to drop this amendment?
May I ask both the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Justice to look carefully at the effect of my suggestion. If they dropped the proposal to have the present amendment adopted and, in the place of that, introduced an amending section which would contain any specific provisions they saw fit in regard to the number of race heats permitted and so on, but, in so far as this question of the cost is concerned, deleted the words in the old section, "at the expense of the association", then they would leave the section so that there would be permission to carry on these activities under the supervision of the Department of Agriculture. As has been pointed out by the minister, this will be mainly done by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, who are already engaged for the general service of the government in the enforcement of our law.
This is not a case of suggesting any reckless expenditures of money. It is true that the estimated cost of the supervision that has been carried on is something in excess of $200,000. The government has raised many amendments to the Criminal Code that have automatically imposed an expense of a much larger sum of money. We have all supported those amendments in the belief that they were good amendments and that the activities of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police or other enforcement bodies should be extended to those activities. I know that what happens here will depend upon the agreement or otherwise of the government, represented in this case by the Minister of Agriculture as the minister piloting this act and the Minister of Justice as the minister mainly responsible for the interpretation and, in the ordinary course of events, the Criminal Code.
Now I leave the situation there. I believe you will be doing the thing that would most help the small fairs and you will be avoiding anything in the way of introduction of an unsatisfactory principle, which is an extension of the beginning that was made by putting the cost on the fairs themselves, if you drop this part of the amendment and bring in an amending section which we will approve, which would strike out the words "at the expense of the association" from the existing section. If the minister is prepared to consider that seriously, then this would be an appropriate point to call it one o'clock and let the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Justice consider this. We will give immediate agreement to that proposal,

Criminal Code
and I think it is consistent with all our law enforcement. The mounted police are there. That will avoid any problem of appointing new officials to go out and collect that money, and it will be consistent with the way in which we bring in new duties to the mounted police from time to time by the introduction of new laws.

For instance, the amount paid on each horse has to be determined.

speechtext: That is done by a machine now.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext: Yes, but an individual has to be there checking the machines.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext: How large is the staff?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext: I cannot give the exact figures, but there needs to be a considerable staff. That staff reports to the police. The reason police are used is that everyone knows that a red coat at a place of that kind is looked upon as just as important as he is around this building. They take it that, if that man is there, as soon as he gets the information that the law has been broken, the race meeting will be stopped by him. They are experts on that. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION

I would point out that not one word that I have said would produce a result that would limit in any way the opportunity for the government, through the Department of Agriculture or the Department of Justice, to enforce the laws. You will not merely be helping the fairs more than you are helping them now by removing any cost of this kind and avoiding this special bookkeeping that would be involved in this procedure and the special supervision that would be involved in it- which in itself is an additional cost-but you would simply be absorbing one of the ordinary cases of the cost of government supervision. I am going to leave the matter there with the suggestion that the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Justice consider this suggestion, and ask that we call it one o'clock.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION

Criminal Code

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PARIMUTUEL BETTING AND SUPERVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the proposal made by the Leader of the Opposition before lunch was that the words "at the expense of the association" in the legislation as it now reads be struck out, and that the proposal which has been made to amend the legislation should also be abandoned. The legislation as it now stands is set out on the righthand sheet of the bill and the words "at the expense of the association" are there. They have been struck out in the amendment and then we have added the latter part reading:
. . . and the person or association conducting a race meeting shall pay to the Receiver General of Canada one-half of one per cent of the total amount of bets made through the agency of a parimutuel system operated under such supervision, on any race run at such meeting.
If you take both of those out, as the Leader of the Opposition suggests, it would simply be a matter of taking money out of the general taxation across the country and spending whatever had to be spent in order to give the service required. The suggestion is that in that way we could give whatever supervision we wished at the small fairs or small racing meets and also give supervision at the larger meets such as those held in Toronto, Winnipeg, Vancouver and elsewhere, and thus charge the whole thing up to the general taxes of the country.
I quite agree that the supervision might be just as good under the one system as under the other, but I do think we would be back into the same kind of discussion we had when the legislation was before the house in its present form years ago. It will be remembered that the person who was minister of justice years ago was a very strong opponent of horse racing and betting of every kind. The legislation was tightened up a great deal at that time and the one exception in the tightening up was in instituting proper supervision of parimutuels and then making those who wager pay the costs. We do not think it is going to be helpful so far as the question of administration of a matter of this kind is concerned to restore it to the position it was in before and ask taxpayers generally, whether or not they believe in racing, to pay the costs of supervision in order to see to it that the law is carried out.
We think it is better that the costs should be charged against the wagers that are made, and therefore we are opposed to doing these two things which would make it absolutely certain that everything would be charged against the general tax rates of the country. I suggest that the figures I produced this morning indicate what that would mean. The costs of the Ontario Jockey Club at Woodbine park, Toronto, are $240 compared with total

Criminal Code
wagering of $304,820, whereas the cost at Humboldt is $40 compared with total wager-ings of $886.
As I understand the suggestion, it is that instead of taking $240 and a little more from Woodbine park we would take the money out of the general taxes, and I do not think that is preferable to what is proposed in the bill. I think it is better to leave the proposal as it is so that the larger race meetings will pay a greater amount than they are now and the smaller ones will pay less. As a matter of fact, the charge is not now made directly against the association. The charge is taken out in the same way that all other charges are. According to the legislation a certain amount is taken out for provincial taxes, a certain amount is taken out to pay prizes and a certain amount is taken out to take care of the expenses of the association. All this proposal means is that another small amount will be taken out of the total wager-ings in order to level out the costs over the whole system so that the small race meet will pay less and the big race meet will pay more.
The whole thing is based on the idea that the supervision is a good thing. People come to see me complaining about things that may happen, and no matter in what way they are interested, whether they are interested because they wager, whether they are interested because they own horses, whether they are interested because they own a race track, they all say the supervision is a good thing. They all want it carried on just as effectively as it has been carried on. They all say they would not like to see themselves in the position where it was carried on under any other system, that this is the best system we have ever had. They say that they want to see the same supervision at every point where racing is carried on under the parimutuel system. They want to see supervision there and therefore they are prepared to see to it that some of the money wagered should go toward that purpose rather than for other purposes. Now, that is all the bill means, and that is all that is in it. I do not see how it can be made any better, and I am suggesting we pass it as it is.
