subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I hope that my colleagues in the house, as well as yourself, will be indulgent with me if, in saying a few words, I thereby delay prorogation of this session, something that can be legitimately longed for at this time of the year. I would have liked to set an example by remaining silent, but I deem it my duty as a member of the house and as a lawyer to stress the reasons and the motives likely to show the soundness and desirability of this step taken by our government, to ensure better administration of justice in Canada.
I shall try to be as brief, concise and logical as possible. May I say that I am not taking part in this debate to foster the interests of any particular group of society with which I am associated professionally. On this occasion I am not moved by any personal interest, either direct or indirect. On the contrary, in expressing my humble opinion, my sole purpose is to avail myself of a prerogative dear to all people interested in promoting the common weal.
Need I point out, Mr. Chairman, that by its constitution, the state has three essential powers to ensure its smooth administration in peace, order and justice. These are legislative power, executive power and judicial power.
The matter before the house today deals with this latter power, which is essential to the Canadian nation. It should not be brushed aside inconsiderately, or still less for some unavowable or unavowed motives, which would give rise, among the public, to sophistical arguments, provoke a clash between classes, disrupt social order and do irreparable damage to society itself. The duty of those who, like us, are members of the legislative power, is not to jeopardize public order but rather to foster the common good.

Society comes from God, like man himself and all other beings in the universe. It is governed by infallible and imprescriptible laws which cannot be violated without upsetting established order. Nor is society possible without an efficient authority capable of enforcing respect for the rights of the individual and of turning the collective will towards the pursuit of the same ideal; otherwise it would mean anarchy and the arbiters of nations could not administer justice.
But this authority which, by its laws, defines the rights of individuals is not allpowerful. It has its limits. It would be useless to tell a citizen that, in certain circumstances, he can do as he likes if others are not bound to respect his right. The legislator must ensure, by penalties, the exercise of individual rights; otherwise the law would fail of its purpose and would no longer be a principle of order. This is where justice comes in. Without this combined protection and coercion, the strong would crush the weak and no society would be possible.
We know that there are three kinds of justice: commutative, distributive and legal.
Commutative justice compels the individual to respect the rights of others. Distributive justice apportions the obligations, favours, honours and obligations of the members of society. As for legal justice, according to St. Thomas, the evangelic doctor, "It governs the relations of individuals with society, setting them in order and adjusting them for the common good. It is legal justice which leads good citizens into accepting the sacrifices necessary to the common good while, at the same time, it inspires statesmen with zeal and directs them in their solicitude for all that may contribute to it."
Justice is therefore the bulwark of the citizen's liberty, as there can be no efficient justice without freedom and no real freedom in society without justice. Justice serves mankind. It teaches that right takes precedence over power. Its administration is entrusted to the bench whose members must set themselves as "the echo of the law" and must identify themselves with the ideal pursued by the legislator, "for justice means to give to each his own." At all times and in every country, artists have personified justice as holding scales in her hand and armed with a sword, a symbol of peace, wealth and happiness. Justice and peace go hand in hand.
Without justice, there is confusion in law, and without law there can be no order. Can peace, abundance and happiness prevail without order?

Administering justice in this world is a great and noble undertaking. The work of a judge is a heavy responsibility, and it is often extremely difficult to perform. It nevertheless remains sublime since a judge's decision is a manifestation of that divine will of which human law is the expression. Even more than that, justice, as administered by the courts, is the "guardian and servant of charity". There can be no charity in disorder and it is to justice that we must look for the establishment and maintenance of order.
Mr. Chairman, before proceeding to a discussion of the subject matter of the bill which the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) has had the courage and the goodness to submit to this house, I have deemed it my duty to set out the basis of my argument and to remind hon. members briefly of the division of power in the state and of the part that authority plays in society, to define justice, its necessity in this world and its inseparability from charity, order and peace. All this I have done in order to emphasize the importance of the matter now under consideration and the seriousness of our responsibilities in this connection.
Integrity, independence and firmness, qualities which those amenable to justice require of magistrates, imply preparation, training, culture, improvement and work on the part of the latter. Any honest man, in these times when so much feverish activity is devoted to the acquisition of wealth, must feel relieved to know that we still can find unselfish men, of unquestioned knowledge and erudition who, for a nominal and so far inadequate salary, are willing to spend the rest of their life in administering justice in an impartial way. Their conscience is a safeguard for this country and a guarantee that the rule of law will be upheld. If incompetence must not endanger the common good, neither must this common good be endangered by financial insecurity.
That is why, Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to give my humble support to this bill. It is well known that in Canada today, and especially in the province of Quebec where I live, the number of judges is inadequate, as well as their salary. I congratulate the Minister of Justice for his determination to improve the condition of those under his "jurisdiction" and I do hope that the competent authorities will undertake to improve the fate of the others and to increase the judiciary.
No one will deny that our natural resources are undergoing such an extraordinary development that, while the population is growing, it tends to converge more and more 50433-325J
Judges Act
towards the cities. So it is, for instance, that 50 years ago the population of the province of Quebec did not exceed 1,648,898 and the number of judges of the superior court was 32. In 1952, the population had reached 4,174,000 but the number of judges had been increased to 46 only.
At the time, as we can see, the population increased by 153 per cent while the number of judges increased by only 31 per cent. And, of course, the Quebec population has kept on increasing these last three years, but the same cannot be said for the number of judges. It can be logically inferred that the number and the importance of disputes at law 'have greatly increased and that, consequently, the work and the responsibilities of the judiciary have also increased.
But that is not all. Fifty years ago the salary of judges of the superior courts and the queen's bench courts in the province of Quebec was $5,000 a year, and income tax had not yet been introduced. Today, apart from taxes and increased work, the cost of living is more than four times what it was, so that in fact our judges are in a position where their predecessors at the turn of the century were twice as well off as they. However, comparisons are generally futile. And yet, may I be allowed to add that it is high time that some consideration was given to the matter of putting the salaries of the judiciary on an equal basis with those of the heads of large commercial firms, whether public or private, without mentioning the special privileges that are benefiting the latter. Society does not attach so much importance to the number of rulings as to the wisdom of these rulings. On the other hand, wisdom can only come from thought, which is only possible in calm, serene and secure surroundings. And in order to be free from material worry, the judiciary must get fair salaries. According to some author "whoever in this world does a superior job is a superior man."
This fair salary, Mr. Chairman, is the basis of the satisfactory operation of justice, which is indispensable to the domestic security of nations and to their stability. We all have a part to play in the search for our common welfare and to that end we must be the friends of the law which, for society, is at the root of all order, peace, prosperity and happiness.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say just a few words on clause 1 in keeping with what I said yesterday. At that time I made the statement that I believed the present scale of salaries for judges was

Judges Act
quite in keeping with the salaries paid to those in the public service of Canada. I admit that it is necessary that we have judges in this country with wide training and experience, and after listening to some of the legal arguments advanced in this house I am more convinced than ever that such is the case.
However, let us look at what some of these appointments carry with them. I shall refer only to those in the lowest bracket, receiving $8,000 a year. They are in receipt of expense allowances of from $12 to $15 per day while on duty. They are in receipt of pensions on a non-contributory basis, with the pension continuing to the widow should she survive. On top of that there is a certain degree of permanency; unless there is some misbehaviour on their part they are assured of a permanent position until they reach the age of 75 years.
So, considering everything, we are still convinced that the scale of salaries paid to our judges is in keeping with salaries paid to those in the public service of Canada. Therefore at this time we are still expressing our opposition to any increases in salaries.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I hesitate to criticize or oppose increases in salaries because I think they are a sign and symbol which is all to the good for the general pride and national well-being of Canada. However, in British Columbia we have what is largely a package deal. There is to be a new appointment to the appellate court and an additional appointment to the supreme court. Because of our increasing population there is considerable additional litigation in our courts.
However, if my memory serves me correctly these judges receive an additional $1,500 or $1,600 from the provincial administration, which brings up their salaries by that amount. On top of that, as has been mentioned by several hon. members, they come under a non-contributory pension scheme. Further, if they are away from their circuits in some other part of the province they are paid their expenses for such time as they are away. It seems to me that under such circumstances a flat increase of $2,500 is unjustified.
Truly I am quite in sympathy with the district court judges, and I am desirous of seeing their salaries increased by the amount set out in the bill, $2,500. I understand that here in the province of Ontario the district court judge is possibly treated with more respect than is the queen's bench judge. I do not know about that, but that is what I hear. He becomes more or less a squire

in the community, and many of the people passing him in the street doff their hats and address him as "Judge".
In British Columbia, the province from which I happen to come, that condition does not prevail. The supreme court judge there is, I would say, regarded at least on an equal basis with the district court judge, if not above him. In my experience of practically 30 years of residence in British Columbia, I do not know of any potential judicial appointments where the Minister of Justice had to twist anybody's arm to get him to accept. I do not think conditions will prevail in the next few years which will cause that situation to come about. As a matter of fact I can think of several dozen lawyers right now in British Columbia who would practically give their right arms to become judges of the supreme court, to say nothing of the appellate division.
In view of the situation it seems to me, when they are now getting $14,400 a year, this increase is not required. It is not required as far as their financial status in the community is concerned, and it is not required as far as the ability of the Minister of Justice to secure additional appointments to the bench is concerned. I noticed that this morning's Globe and Mail takes the government to task because the suggested increase is not as much as it should be. The Globe and Mail states that it should be on a percentage basis and, additionally, that it should be 50 per cent over and above the increase being given at the present time.
There is another factor that comes into this picture. Some of the learned judges of the supreme court will tell you that they have to live a very isolated existence. Maybe they do. Truly they cannot be seen at gatherings with men and women who may be going to appear before them the following morning on criminal charges; but by and large the life of a supreme court justice in any province of Canada is one that almost anyone in this house would rather enjoy.
As far as I personally am concerned I feel that this additional increase is not justified at this time. As I said, my objections, unfortunately, come into the category of a parcel deal. I am in favour of the district court judge getting this increase but, for those learned gentlemen from the supreme court up through the exchequer court to the Supreme Court of Canada, I cannot see that we are justified in making this increase at this time.
I believe I am right in saying that as far as Canada is concerned, the man who should be paid the highest salary in this country is the Prime Minister. The responsibilities of his office and the relationship he has to maintain

with all the people in Canada in my opinion justify an increase to far above what the Prime Minister is now receiving in indemnity or salary from the people of Canada. Consequently, in conclusion, though I have expressed my lack of desire to oppose increases in salaries in all vocations of life, I feel that this increase at this time is quite unjustified, and I would hope the government might reconsider this package deal. They should certainly give the district court judges an increase, but when it comes to the present holders of other judicial positions in the superior courts of Canada, we could well drop the increase at this time.

I should like to endorse what has already been stated as the position of this group by my colleague from Winnipeg North Centre. As a matter of fact I should like to endorse what has just been said by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, whose arguments were very logical. Let me say in the first place that I believe the proposed increases would make too great a gap between the salaries of judges and the salary of the average citizen of this country.
I am well aware of the arguments that could be advanced against that statement. I shall be told that a judge is not an ordinary citizen of the country. But, after all, it is the average citizen of this country who has to pay his taxes in order that these salaries may be paid. Like the gentleman whom I have already mentioned, I have no objection to the $2,500 increase in the salaries of those who are now in receipt of $8,000.
The argument has been advanced that the higher salaries are necessary for the better administration of justice. That argument does not appeal to me at all. To say that honesty and integrity can be preserved only by paying higher salaries to the very fine men who are judges at the present time is an allegation which certainly I personally am not prepared to make, though it has been advanced as an argument for the granting of such increases.
I have before me a list of the present salaries and a list of the salary increases as proposed by this bill. I shall not take the highest bracket, but I shall take the bracket with the present salary of $20,000. The new salary proposed by this bill is $22,500, and I notice that across from that the pension scale which is $10,666 for the judge himself and $3,555 for his widow. I understand that according to the legislation now on the order paper the $10,666 in this particular case would not be reduced in order to give the widow
Judges Act
a greater pension. If this judge were unfortunate enough to lose his wife he still would be entitled, after remarriage, to a pension of $10,666.
I am not going to review the other figures, though I have them before me, except to mention the last one, which is $8,000. I think it might be reasonably raised to the $10,500 stated in the legislation; and even here there is a corresponding rather satisfactory pension of $5,333 for the man himself, with the widow's pension being $1,777. For these reasons I am prepared to oppose the legislation, except the last part with regard to the district court judges.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not think that the members of the House of Commons can complain that I have inflicted upon them any great amount of oratory in connection with the passage of this bill. I said at the resolution stage that I thought the bill was self-explanatory and self-justifying.
However, in view of the remarks which have been made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, the hon. member for Saskatoon, the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke and the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard I think that I would not be discharging my duty as Minister of Justice if I did not point out certain facts which, it seems to me, should be upon the record if it is to be a well-balanced one.
What we are dealing with here is our endeavour to maintain, under present modern-day conditions, courts well staffed with competent judges. We all know that, as the years go by, the business of individuals, corporations, provincial governments and federal governments all grows in complexity and importance and that the amounts of money involved increase. The conduct of that business-whether it be the management of private concerns or corporations, or of municipalities, or of provincial governments or of the federal government-requires a wider knowledge and greater talent, training and skill. This, of course, is likewise true of the litigation which arises in the conduct of that business.
From the remarks that have been made by each one of the four hon. members to whom I have referred it is clear that they have a most inadequate comprehension of the qualities which a top-grade counsel must possess. From experience in dealing with such men I suggest to them that in order that a man be a top-grade counsel he must, first of all, possess a mind which is penetrating and powerful not only within the confines of his own study, but he must be able

Judges Act
public life. I want to make a flat contradiction of that statement. If the hon. member had taken the pains to examine the facts before he made the statement he would have found that even after these proposed increases go into effect there will be a number of deputy ministers in the service who will still be getting more money than a supreme court judge. To name them, they are the deputy ministers of agriculture, external affairs, finance, justice, national defence, trade and commerce, and the clerk of the privy council. I say, sir, that, properly discharged by a competent man, the duties of a judge of the high court are at least as important in our society as those of the deputy ministers I have named.
I think that is all I have to say upon these points that have been raised.

It is not only a valid argument, but it is relevant to the question we are discussing, as to whether we should be making these increases at this time. I do not blame the Minister of Justice for finding a good quotation, if he can, from a man for whom I have the greatest of respect, Mr. Clement Attlee, the leader of the Labour party of the United Kingdom. But I suggest there are several differences between the situation there and the situation here which have a bearing on the picture. I understand, for example, that there is a rigid line drawn in the United Kingdom between barristers and solicitors, and that it is members of one of the groups who move up into the position of judges, and not members of the other.
Then the Minister of Justice likes to tell us, when he is pinch-hitting for the Minister of Finance, that income tax rates are much higher in the United Kingdom than they are here, and particularly in the higher brackets. I have heard the same Mr. Attlee tell the story of how little was taken in income tax years ago in the United Kingdom, and how the picture now is completely reversed whereby there are some individuals in the United
[Mr. Garson.l
Kingdom today who have left the amount they paid in income tax some years ago.
I agree, as the minister does, with the contention of Mr. Attlee that we should be paying the right remuneration to our judges. It is our contention that in the light of our scales of salaries, in the light of the pension privileges, and in the light of the prestige enjoyed by these people, salaries of $14,400 up to $25,000 per year are nearer the correct figure we should be paying than would be the higher figures proposed in this bill. The minister is aware of the fact-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

I would be delighted to answer that question. Because of the fact that men in the public service, civil servants, politicians and judges, are paid on a uniformly lower scale than those in commercial life, the Prime Minister is paid a lesser amount than the president of the Canadian National Railways. I entirely agree with the hon. member that, ideally, he should be paid very much more. The question I am asking him is as to two persons, both engaged in the public service. When he says that one has the

responsibility of the head of a department, he should remember that the other man also has the responsibility of protecting our freedom and of standing out against the executive if necessary. What surprises me more than anything else in this debate is that the members of the opposition, who should be more interested than anyone else in protecting the position of the judges in the land, are the ones who are attacking it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I object. Surely the minister has reached the end of his argument when he says we are attacking judges, or that we are attacking those who are defending our freedom. I say we do not think a price tag should be put on this sort of thing. I have already mentioned the Prime Minister and I will mention as well his colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce. If those two gentlemen had stayed out of politics and remained in private life, I believe everyone agrees they would be making far more money than they are today. Was it a price tag that brought them into parliament? Is it a price tag that keeps them here? It is the concept of service that keeps them here, whether or not we agree with the form of service they are rendering. I give them both full credit for the fact that they are prepared to take less than they might make otherwise, in rendering what they believe to be a service to the country.
I think the same thing applies to our judges. I am not asking that the judges work for nothing. I am not criticizing them. I have the highest regard for them. I had at least one very interesting experience for three days before a judge of one of the superior courts of this country. I remember the experience with a great deal of pleasure, and indeed it was an education that I enjoyed greatly. I know a number of judges personally, and my respect for them is very high. But I submit it is not going to make the difference between getting or not getting these high-priced lawyers-that is apparently the mark of high calibre-by increasing these salaries to the figures suggested.
The Minister of Justice is aware of the fact that some time soon, because of a recent death, he is going to have to make an appointment to the position of chief justice of the supreme court of British Columbia. I do not know whether he makes it or recommends it, but at any rate he has something to do with it. I ask him, would he have any more difficulty getting a thoroughly suitable person for that job at $16,000 a year than he would at $18,500?
The minister nods his head. I am sure the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard does
Judges Act
not agree with him. I am sure he agrees with me that at $16,000 a year there are plenty of lawyers, not just run of the mill but good, capable jurists, who would be glad to take that job. They would take it not just because of the $16,000 and the pension that goes with it, or the security, but because it coincides with their interests, because they can render a service, and because they can enjoy the high regard which is accorded to men in that position.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not want to prolong this debate unnecessarily, and I greatly appreciate the very thorough way the minister dealt with our opposition to this particular item. However, I do believe there are a couple of points at least upon which he has not touched.
The minister spoke about it being so necessary that judicial appointments be made from counsel of extremely high calibre. I do not know how the people feel in the province of Ontario or in the other provinces of Canada, but in the years that have elapsed since I returned from the first world war I have seen in the various provinces in which I have lived many men appointed to high judicial positions.
I have found by observation that it is not a hard and fast rule that top-flight corporation counsel make good judges. I have seen, as I am sure many hon. members have seen, judges appointed from barristers at law who were by no means high-class; yet after they were appointed to the bench they became, in many instances, more studious, more efficient, and better able to render proper judicial decisions than the men who had been in so-called high corporation and counsel practices. That to me is not an absolute essential so far as requirements for appointment to the bench are concerned.
I rather feel that we are getting a bit confused on this issue when we bring freedom into the picture. That is an extraneous issue that should not be brought into the picture at all. However, the Minister of Justice made a point with respect to a strong bench, and a strong bar and a weak bench. I would not like to see that happen. Despite that possibility I still maintain my position, Mr. Chairman. Though my head may be bloody it is still unbowed, despite the assertion of the Minister of Justice.
We have seen in this parliament with respect to a certain department of government that the bar has not shown up too well. There are still many able members of the bar in Canada. There will be in the days to come as there have been in the days gone by. Whether you increase the emolument or indemnity you will still find among the

Judges Act
ablest members of the bar men who are very-happy to accept judicial appointment above that of a district court judge.
I do not want to continue at length on this theme, but it seems to me where they have not had an increase for some 150 years, as the Minister of Justice pointed out was the case in the United Kingdom, something should be done. It is not 150 years by any manner of means since we had an increase in judicial salaries in Canada. As I said in my initial remarks, I certainly do not want it to be thought by anyone either in the house or outside of it that I am opposing increases in salaries, because I am not. But it seems to me that in this situation we can go forward quite adequately without interfering with the sound judgment of the judiciary from the Atlantic to the Pacific. We can do it under the old set-up of wage scales or indemnities and do it to the credit not only of this government and this parliament but to the eternal credit of the people of Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am in a kind of predicament. I was allowed to come down here on the express understanding that I would keep my mouth shut. What is going to happen in certain quarters after it is heard that I did not do so, I do not know. I do not believe I would have risen to say a word in this debate were it not for the peculiar idea that seems to be abroad, namely that you can buy everything with money, including justice.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: Who ever said that?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not know that the statement has been made here during this debate, but if it has not been made here during this debate it has been made during similar debates; that judges should be well paid in order that they would be under no temptation to go wrong in the administration of justice. I have heard it said in this house. The minister shakes his head, but I have been here longer than he has and I have heard that statement made. If we accept that statement, then we must admit that most people who go wrong do so because their economic conditions are not what they should be. There is no doubt about it that probably 90 per cent of the cases that come before judges, particularly cases of violence and things of that kind, come before them because of poor upbringing, economic difficulties, and so forth.
I was interested last winter in reading a statement made by a judge in the province of Quebec on sentencing a young man. He regretted the fact that the law allowed him no other course except to send this young man to the penitentiary. He said he would
[Mr. MacDougall.l
have liked to send this young man some place where he would have a chance to start rebuilding his life. He took into consideration his family upbringing and the conditions under which he lived after he left the family. I consider that was a good judge. A judge in Vancouver said something similar just the other day.
I should not like anyone to feel that I have not a high regard for the judges of this country. I have said on many occasions in this house, when statements were made that judges should not be allowed to sit on boards, commissions, conciliation boards and things of that kind, that I am all in favour of their being allowed to do so, because we probably get from a judge in such a position a valuation of the issue involved that we could not get from any other person.
As to appointments, I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard that unfortunately the calibre of the person and his qualifications are not the only things that are taken into consideration in appointing judges. Of course I do not say that ability and fitness are not considered.
I have mentioned this before, and probably the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra will not mind my mentioning it again. In 1935 the hon. member was opposed by a lawyer. Of course both candidates could not be elected and the Liberal candidate, the lawyer, was defeated. He was later appointed to the bench. Why was he appointed? Was it because he was an outstanding lawyer? Certainly not. I am not going to comment upon it, but I would not make an affidavit on it that he also is an outstanding judge. Then in 1940 the hon. member again had a lawyer for his opponent. The hon. member was elected, the lawyer was defeated, and before very long he, too, was made a judge.
This is not something that happens infrequently; it happens quite often. Unfortunately, judgeships are sometimes considered to be for lame ducks. We may as well accept it that such is the case. I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard that sometimes persons who have not shown very great ability when practising at the bar have shown good judgment when promoted to the bench.
I do not believe that justice or freedom or any of these things depend upon the salaries paid to the judges in the higher courts. When you take into consideration the salaries judges receive, the pensions, the pensions received by their widows, it must be agreed that not only are they in a good position, they are in a favourable position as compared with other residents of this country. They are in that favourable position without the present proposed salary increases.

If we are going to improve the quality of society, and I hope that is what we are here for, we must do so not by improving the position of those at the top but by improving the condition of those at the bottom. Otherwise we will never improve society; we will never lift society above what it is now and judges will be faced with the same problems they are faced with now, of sentencing young men and women to penitentiaries and jails when they know they will come out of those places much worse people than when they went in.
I should like to mention the case of a young boy of 14 years who was sentenced to the penitentiary for stealing a car. He had been in one of our provincial reform institutions and with some other young boys about the same age he took a car, was captured, brought to court and sentenced. There was an editorial about it a few days go in the Vancouver Province. The judge said there was nothing he could do but sentence the boy to the penitentiary for whatever the term was, two years or more. The Province is a staid and reasonable paper, and it made reference to what the position of that boy would be after he had associated during the period of his sentence with hardened, habitual criminals. The boy had said he wanted to be sent to the penitentiary in order to learn a trade, but the only trade he will learn will be that of crime and more crime. When he comes out he will be in worse condition than when he went in. If we are going to do something to better society we have to begin with these boys, not with the judges who pass sentence upon them.

speechtext:
Clause 3 is the one that sets the salary rates for the judges of the courts of appeal in the provinces, and also for the county court judges. A moment ago the minister said it was correct, as far as his recollection went, that the three provinces which pay additional amounts are British Columbia, Manitoba and Ontario. Initially I was disposed to disagree with him in so far as British Columbia was concerned, but I recall now that we do have a statute there that provides for the payment of an additional amount to judges.
What I had in mind, however, was rather the provision, such as is the practice in Ontario, that the county court judges are entitled to receive additional remuneration for their surrogate work, which is not the case in British Columbia. Our countv court judges, who have most of the powers of a supreme court judge in probate in those areas where there is no supreme court judge, get no additional remuneration whatsoever for that work.
That brings me to the point I mentioned yesterday in the discussion on the resolution. I said I felt that it would be well for the minister to call into conference the attorneys general of the provinces and discuss with them this problem of equalizing, as far as it can be done, the burden of work which falls on judges of comparable positions, and to some extent equalizing the remuneration by advocating some uniform practice with respect to the additional emoluments which sometimes come to the judges. My colleague from London, I know, has given a great deal of study to this matter and I am not going to go into it in detail. I shall leave him in a few moments to discuss the matter with the minister. I just wanted to refer to the suggestion I made yesterday, which I did not

press at that time. Before this clause is carried I would appreciate hearing from the minister on that point.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure my hon. friend from Kamloops realizes that the federal government has constitutional responsibility for the appointment of all judges of provincial and federal courts; but that after such judges have been appointed the responsibility for the manner in which their work is carried on in the provincial courts falls under the heading of administration of justice.
If I may say so, I would be inclined to differ with my hon. friend's suggestion that we should call a conference at which the federal government would take the initiative of suggesting to province A that it should follow a course of conduct in the payment of judges which is followed by province B. To follow this course would not in my view improve dominion-provincial relations to any extent.
I must say, however, that when we had an indirect interest in the case load and the way in which that case load was divided in a given province, which in turn had a bearing upon action which we had to take in the discharge of our own constitutional responsibility, I have not hesitated to discuss, as matters of joint concern to the provincial government and ourselves, the steps that might be taken provincially to get a better distribution of the case load. I must say that I received good co-operation indeed from the provincial authorities. But it requires no imagination to realize that this is a subject matter that must be approached with great discretion if one is to avoid being misunderstood.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Quite so. What I had in mind was not that the dominion government should in any way seek to lay down the law in this field. But since there are discrepancies in the gross remuneration which judges receive, the matter presents certain problems to the minister when he asks or contemplates asking this committee to make a uniform increase in judges' salaries across Canada. We know perfectly well, as does the minister, that judges in various parts of the country holding comparable appointments not only have greatly varying work loads but are in receipt also of salaries as to which there is considerable difference; yet he cannot make a differential in the increase that is recommended here.
As I say, the matter presents the government or the department or parliament with a problem. I felt that it would be quite appropriate for the minister to suggest, if
Judges Act
he likes, to the various attorneys general that they meet with him at some convenient time and discuss ways and means of achieving a greater uniformity. It may be found not to be possible but I think an effort should be made.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not wish to hold up this clause, because I support particularly the increase which is proposed for the county court judges. In fact I feel that the gap between what is paid to a county court judge on the one hand and what is paid to superior court judges on the other hand should, if anything, be closed. I am in no way against the increase which has been granted to the superior court judges. If I have any criticism of this bill it is that it has not sufficiently closed the gap between the salaries of county court judges and those of superior court judges.
The practice has been-and increasingly so over the past few years-that county judges are assuming many of the duties formerly carried out by the supreme court judges. That situation has arisen for several reasons. One is that the amount of litigation going through our courts has increased tremendously in the last 10, 12 or 15 years. It is simply impossible, with a reasonable number of judges on the supreme court bench, to deal with all the cases there are to be dealt with.
The second point I should like to make with respect to county judges is this, and it also applies to some remarks that were made by some hon. gentlemen with respect to supreme court judges when they referred several times to the question of buying justice. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the question of increasing the salaries of either class of judges is not a case of buying justice but simply a case of how much we are prepared to ask these men to accept by way of sacrifice in order to perform a service. Are we prepared to ask them to accept a larger sacrifice than that which is at present accepted? I think not. That sacrifice is particularly noticeable in the case of county judges.
I cannot establish this fact from the papers I have in front of me-the minister will undoubtedly correct me if I am wrong-but some years ago county court judges were paid on approximately the same basis as were deputy ministers. I shall have something to say in connection with pensions, which were referred to by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre on section 8, I think it is, of the act. But we have been discussing the comparative salary scales as between superior court judges and senior members of the civil

Judges Act
service. We are now down to the case of the county court judge, who some years ago was on a par with a senior civil servant, but who is now away below par.

speechtext: The hon. member for London asked me to correct him. My own records go back only as far as 1919, but I think that is quite a distance back. At that time the county or district court judges received $4,000 and nearly all the deputy ministers received $5,000. That is a difference of about 25 per cent.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: May I ask the minister to turn to page 2 for a moment? There we find set out, under the salaries of the judges of the supreme court of New Brunswick an amount for "the judge of the court of divorce and matrimonial causes". It does not appear in any other section. What has that to do with?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: That is an additional amount that is paid to one of the superior court judges for acting as judge of divorce and matrimonial causes; that is for looking after divorce cases.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: Do not other judges look after them?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: No, I do not think so; not in that province.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: What about the other provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: As my hon. friend knows, in the province of Ontario-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: Yes, I know the situation in the province of Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: -and in the province of Manitoba and also, I believe, in nearly ail the other provinces, all superior court judges take divorces.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: I have just one other comment I wish to make. Some reference has already been made to the fact that the increase now authorized for county court and supreme court judges-in fact, for all judges affected [DOT]-is across the board, a flat increase, as against the percentage increase which was the pattern in the last two cases, to my recollection.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: No; the previous cases were a percentage.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: That is what I say; the previous cases were percentage increases.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: It is now a flat or across the board increase as against a percentage increase in the last two cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: I should like to express approval of that pattern, and to commend what was said a moment ago by my colleague the hon. member for London. Since the trend is toward increasing the jurisdiction of county courts, so long at least as that trend continues-and I imagine it will continue for a good length of time-certainly we should not go back to the system of percentage increases which serves only to increase the disparity. I think the emphasis now should be rather on closing the gap between the salaries. These across the board increases have a tendency in that direction.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: Shall the clause carry?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: On division.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: I wish to say a word on section 3, which deals with county court judges. I agree with the remarks made by the hon. member for London. I want to express to the minister my regret that as to the county court judges' salaries he did not see fit to go as far as the bar association recommended, or as far as was recommended in the brief submitted by the county judges' association. Even with the increase of 25 per cent across the board, in my opinion there is still too wide a gap between the salary paid to a county court judge and that paid to a judge of the superior court.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: There is a 31.25 per cent increase in connection with county court judges.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext:
The increase is $2,500. I would point out that it is an increase across the board, and that there is still a wide gap between the increased salaries of county court judges and those of judges of the superior court.
As the minister is aware, in Ontario the county court, by consent, has the same jurisdiction in practically every subject as has the supreme court, with the exception of divorce and certain major matters under the Criminal Code, such as murder, treason, rape and things of that nature. I would point out to the minister as an example that in the county in which I reside, when I started to practise we had two county court judges and a local master of the supreme court. Today we have one county court judge; there is no second judge, nor is there a local master of the supreme court.
The population of my county is approaching 100,000. To give the minister an idea of the amount of work passing through our county court, I have here a list of the cases set down for hearing for the session that

started on the 6th of June this year. There are four criminal cases with a jury. The first criminal case took eight days, and it was estimated that at least three days would be required for each of the other three criminal cases. Then there are eight civil cases to be tried before a jury, and it is anticipated that will take at least to the end of July. When they are disposed of there are 18 nonjury cases. I point that out to the minister and those hon. members who say that county court judges have ample time and do not have enough work to keep them busy.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: The minister did not say that.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext:
No, but I
am pointing it out to the minister. How can any hon. member expect the judge in the county of Hastings to attempt to handle a list like that and carry on all the work that ordinarily passes across a judge's desk? In addition he also has twelve division courts to cover.
The minister mentioned the salaries of various civil servants. If he goes over the list carefully he will find that not only deputy ministers but a great many other senior civil servants are at the present time receiving salaries much in excess of what county court judges will receive even after the increase of $2,500 brings them up to a salary of $10,500. I do not think it is unfair to say that the authority vested in a county court judge is at least equal in importance, and in my opinion far more important, than the authority vested in any of these deputy ministers or other officials. After all, as somebody mentioned, a county court judge has jurisdiction over our liberty. He also has jurisdiction over many other things, and I do not think it is unfair to suggest to the minister that the salaries of county court judges should at least be on a par with those paid to deputy ministers and other senior civil servants.
In replying to an hon. member the minister also mentioned something about the salaries paid to judges in various courts in the United States. I think the minister will agree that the salaries paid there in what correspond to our county and superior courts are, even with the increases being granted by this measure, greatly in excess of what are being paid in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: I think that will depend a great deal upon the state to which my hon. friend is referring. Some of them are quite a bit lower, and of course some of them are higher. The federal salaries are certainly higher.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext:
The federal salaries are higher and, as the minister knows, there are many states where the
Judges Act
salaries are a great deal higher than what will be paid in Canada even with the increases. However, I commend the minister for making the increases, even though they are not as great as I had hoped they would be. I presume it is too late for him to change his mind and bring county court judges up to the level where I think they should be.
I think I should also point out to the minister that at least in eastern Ontario there is a system in operation whereby the judges rotate. There are four judges on the circuit. When one county judge has a great deal of work he is assisted in that work by the judge in the adjoining county, and so on. Whether the same system applies in other provinces I am not sure, but I quite realize that is something within the jurisdiction of the provincial governments.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: Shall the clause carry?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext:
On division.
Clause agreed to on division.
Clause 4 agreed to.
On clause 5-Annuity upon retirement at age 75 years, judges of federal courts.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Under clause 5, which
amends section 24 of the act, I think it would be appropriate to put on the record what this section does by way of establishing a pension schedule, so the picture will be complete for those who may wish to study the matter. If I may say so, without speaking about a clause we have not reached yet, I am glad to note that the minister has put in a provision which will have the effect of preventing any increases in pensions consequent upon the increase in salary.
I shall have to qualify that statement when we get to another clause, but I think it should be pointed out here that we are providing for our judges pensions equal to two-thirds of the salary they are now drawing. I understand that even after the salary increase the pension will be two-thirds of the present salary, and not two-thirds of the new salary. That means we are providing as a pension for the chief justice of the Supreme Court of Canada the sum of $16,666 a year. For the associate or puisne judges of that court the pension will be $13,333. The pension for the president of the Exchequer Court of Canada and for the chief justices of each of the various superior courts of the provinces will be $10,666 a year. The pension for the associate justices of the Exchequer Court of Canada and the associate justices of all superior courts of the provinces will be $9,600 a year. The pension for county court

Judges Act
judges will be $5,333 a year. Those are the figures which now obtain; this clause continues them.
There is also the matter of the provision for widows, but that comes under a later clause so I shall leave any comment on it until we have reached the appropriate clause. Since the Hansard record for yesterday and today contains a good many of the facts I felt that it should also contain as part of the total picture the pensions we make available to our judges on a non-contributory basis.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Clause agreed to.
On clause 6-Annuity to widows.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: Is subsection 3 of the proposed new section entirely new?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: No, it is not new. It is subsection 5 of section 27 of the existing Judges Act.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like to say a word with regard to clause 6 and the amending job it does on section 27 of the act. I have tried to read the clause very carefully, and if in what I say I indicate I have misunderstood it I hope the minister will correct me immediately. That is one hope I can count on being fulfilled; I am very sure of that.
At the present time section 27 makes what I think is quite a fair provision, so long as you start with the basic premise of a certain size of a pension for a judge. The provision is that a judge may elect to have his pension divided into two parts, one part being two-thirds of the pension, which is for himself, and the other part being one-third of the pension, which is for his wife. If the judge so elects and then dies while on pension, the amount that is his wife's continues as long as she lives. On the other hand, if the wife dies first the judge knows that he will have to get along on two-thirds of his pension after the death of his wife. At the present time the judge has the right to elect that or not elect it. He knows that if his wife dies first he will have less than would otherwise be the case. The satisfaction he gets in return is the knowledge that if he dies first there will be a pension for his widow.
The rates of pension for widows under these circumstances are as follows: $5,555 in the case of the widow of a chief justice of the Supreme Court of Canada; $4,444 in the case of widows of associate justices of the Supreme Court of Canada; $3,555 in the case of widows of the president of the Exchequer Court of Canada or the chief justices of the superior courts of the provinces; $3,200 per year in the case of widows of associate justices of the Exchequer Court of Canada

and associate justices of the provincial superior courts; $1,777 a year in the case of the widows of judges of the county courts.
Let me go back for a moment. I think the picture at the present time is very clear. The judge elects, and two-thirds of his pension is his and one-third is his wife's. As a matter of fact, I believe while both are living they are actually paid that way, two-thirds to him and one-third to the wife. It is crystal clear, therefore, that whoever dies first the other pension continues. As I understand clause 6, however, this business of election is being discontinued and the matter is being put on a fixed basis. The provision will be that the judge will get the full amount of the pension whether or not his wife is alive at the time he goes on pension. As I read it, it would also seem to follow that that full pension continues even though his wife may die. It still holds that the widow gets her one-third of the pension or a corresponding amount if the judge dies while in office. But I think it should be pointed out that if I understand this correctly, whereas a moment ago I congratulated the minister on putting in a clause that prevents the increase in salary from increasing the pension he has by this clause made what virtually is an increase in the judge's pension.
At the present time a chief justice of a provincial superior court, if he has elected, draws a pension of $7,111 and his wife a pension of $3,555. If one or the other dies, the other pension continues. Under the new arrangement the pension of the widow, if she becomes a widow, will be the same, $3,555, but the pension of the judge will be the full $10,666, whether or not his wife is alive.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: Oh, no, not whether his wife is alive and pensioned or not; that would convey a quite wrong impression. Under the new arrangement, since there is no election, the judge gets his full pension and he continues to get it, whether or not his wife is living, until he dies.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: That is just what I said; if after he dies she survives, she gets one-third. I was saying it was $3,555.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: I am sorry; I thought my friend said that a judge gets his pension and the wife gets her pension as well.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext:
It is quite clear that the two pensions are not paid at the same time. This particular judge, who at the present time is guaranteed a pension of $7,111, knowing that the other amount is paid only if his wife is living, now has it guaranteed to him as long as he lives whether or not his wife is alive, that his pension will be $10,666, which is quite a substantial increase.

Now, Mr. Chairman, I know that members across the way do not like this reference. I know I can only make it as a relevant argument, and I cannot go into it. But I submit that as long as this government refuses to raise the old age pension from $40 a month it has no right to be increasing the pension of a man whose salary will now be $18,500 from the present figure of $7,111 to $10,666 per year. I submit that though the words the minister used yesterday are technically correct he did not tell the whole story. He said, as recorded at page 5075 of Hansard for June 21, 1955:
As in the case of the increase in judicial salaries in Great Britain last year, there will be no increase in pensions paid to Canadian judges consequent upon the increase in their salaries as provided in this bill.
That statement is quite correct. There is no increase consequent upon the increase in salaries, but there is an increase in the total pension of a judge on the basis of clause 6.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: All that has been done in this case, as I am sure my hon. friend is the first member of this house to know, is to bring the pension arrangements of the judges into accord with those which prevail for all civil servants.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: But the civil servant's pension is on a contributory basis, and this does not correspond to it at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: I am saying, in respect of this subject matter my hon. friend is discussing. In other words, in most cases where provision is made for pensions to continue to the widow, the usual arrangement is for the man to get it for his life and after his death a half or, as in this case, one-third goes to his widow. It is not a costly arrangement to the treasury and it is an arrangement which, on the basis of experience, we think will work out very well and to the advantage of all concerned.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: I am not objecting to the pension provided for judges' widows. I am not objecting to the principle-in fact I support the principle-of a survivor's pension for the widow. But I think when a judge already has a guaranteed pension, which in the case of the chief justice of a superior court is $7,111 per year for himself and $3,555 for his wife, and is getting an increase in salary from $16,000 to $18,500, he does not need an additional benefit in the form of an increase of over $3,000 in his own pension if he is alive after his wife dies.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I think all members of the house realize that it is not fair to approach this matter simply on the basis on which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has
Judges Act
approached it. It is a fact beyond any question that the pension arrangements have been attractive to the men whose services have been sought on the bench. There is honour attached to being one of Her Majesty's judges. But when men of substantial income have been invited to accept appointment to that high office some of them, faced with a substantial reduction in income, have had to weigh very carefully the pension provisions made for them on their retirement or for their widows against the immediate loss of income in leaving their practice.
Now, two wrongs never make a right. The matter of the old age pension is one to be decided on, its merits. The matter of the judges' pension and the judges' wives' annuities is a matter to be decided on its merits. It seems to me the two are not to be confused in the way the hon. member has approached the problem this afternoon.
There is one aspect of this subject which I have raised previously, as the minister will recall. No provision is made for it in this amendment contained in clause 6 of the bill.
I wish some note had been taken of the problem there. It is a problem, however, that is not going to rise hereafter if section 6 is adopted.
There have been cases where married judges, under the law as it was heretofore, made an election to share their pensions with their wives and outlived their wives. In such cases, the treasury benefited by the election made by the judge, because he submitted on his retirement to a reduction of one-third of the pension he would otherwise have received. I raised this problem at the time of the last increase of the judges' salaries several years ago. I indicated I thought it was not fair in a case of that kind for the treasury to seek to reap a benefit from the death of the wife while the judge was still living. The Minister of Justice indicated he was not prepared at that time to recommend any change in the law to meet that case.
I observe that clause 6 of the bill makes no provision for such cases. There is no provision in clause 6 that is retroactive in any respect. The best that can be said in that regard is that if clause 6 is adopted the problem will not arise in the future. But what I conceive to be an injustice in the case of judges who have already retired does continue to exist. There might not be many such cases, but I do not think it is becoming to the government of this country, where a judge has given faithful service on the bench, often very distinguished service and not infrequently at personal financial sacrifice, that because he has the misfortune to have his wife predecease him, the treasury of this

Judges Act
country should reap a benefit in the form of a reduction of one-third in his pension. In a case of that kind it seems to me it should be open to the judge to receive his full pension notwithstanding the sequence of deaths in the light of the election he had previously made.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: May I ask the minister a question as to the effect of this particular case? My case is hypothetical. I do not know whether or not such a case exists. Suppose there is at the present time a retired judge who under the previous arrangement elected to divide his pension two-thirds for himself and one-third for his wife. Suppose in this case his wife has predeceased him, and he is now drawing just two-thirds of his original pension. What will be the effect on his pension of this clause as amended?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: The answer to my hon. friend's question is that the clause will have no effect if the pension has vested.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: Are these pensions vested? They do not come out of a fund. They are paid on the basis that the governor in council may grant a pension.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: Yes, but once the pension has been granted to the judge and received by him as a judge who has elected and his wife has predeceased him, then it will continue as it was before.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: That was the case I put.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I express my regret that
there is no provision here for dealing with the existing cases. There may not be many of them, but I think I shall go so far as to say it is a shame that advantage is taken of that sequence of deaths where the judge has made his election and retired heretofore.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: I recall the occasion on which that question was debated previously. I thought the hon. gentleman put up a very good case, and I thought I had made an adequate reply on the basis of the act as it stood at that time.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: We never give up.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: I am sure my hon. friend will realize that if we start any retroactive pensions in relation to any of the large number of persons who receive pensions under the government, we are opening up a very large question.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext:
The minister is stating a
broader case than the one I am discussing. He is talking about retroactive reopening of IMr. Fleming.]
pension cases in general, without dealing with the specific case. I wish it very clearly understood that I was dealing with the specific case of a judge who had made his election to share his pension with his wife should she become his widow. He retired either before or after the death of his wife. She predeceased him. That is the case with which I am dealing. I am not speaking about anything stated in broader terms than that. I do not think any such bogey as the minister is raising now should be introduced against an attempt to deal seriously with a specific . problem where it seems to me an injustice is being permitted to continue.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext: As a matter of fact I should like to support the last sentence or two uttered by the hon. member for Eglinton. I do not think these things should be put on the same level. After all, what the hon. member for Eglinton is discussing is the matter of amending the law to change a condition that was basic to the pension. In most of these other cases that are under discussion it is a question as to the rate of pension itself, whether or not it is adequate. In this case it seems to me the hon. member is asking for a person to be given it both ways. The judge in question had the option whether to elect or not. He gambled on the division. He elected in such a way as to leave his widow with a pension if he died first. It turned out the other way. Now apparently he wants to have it the other way as well. Is that not asking to have it both ways?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like to say one or two more brief words in support of the county court judges. I refer back to several remarks made by the minister this afternoon when I was suggesting that the salaries of judges had at one period been somewhat in line with the salaries of deputy ministers and other senior civil servants, and he pointed out to me that there was a difference of $1,000-$4,000 and $5,000-in 1919.
I should like to suggest to the minister that the history of the judges' salaries all through the years since then has been that increases to the judges have followed increases to the civil servants. I am sure the minister will agree with me, when he reads the list of salaries paid in the civil service at the moment, that many civil servants are drawing more than the $8,000 heretofore granted to the judges, and that in some junior ranks of the civil service.
I would suggest that this is a case where the county court judges have, by the very fact of their low salaries, purchased their pensions. My only suggestion here would be that in so far as the county court judges are

concerned, the pensions should be based not on their $8,000 but on their increased salary. I would ask the minister when he speaks to the clause to comment on the truth or otherwise of the statement that the county court judges have, in fact, as a result of their reduced salaries, bought their pensions.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES, PROVIDE FOR JUDGE IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the point which the hon. gentleman raises in relation to the facts is in some respects rather complex. In 1919, as I indicated, most of the deputy ministers were at the $5,000 a year mark. The salary of the county court judges was then $4,000. That was not true, however, of the deputy minister of justice, who then received $10,000, twice as much as the deputy minister of finance. In relation to the responsibilities he carried at that time he was considered to be, and I agree with that idea, worth twice as much as any of the other deputies in relation to the work they then carried on. I might remark in that connection that the deputy minister of justice was engaged, like the judges, in legal work.
What I do suggest is that in many other spheres of governmental activity the responsibilities and the character of the work have changed enormously in the interval between 1919 and 1955. For example, you find that the deputy minister of finance who was paid $5,000 in 1919, in relation to our present-day budgets and all the ramifications of the Department of Finance, is now paid $20,000. Going through the list of deputies you will see that the greatest changes and the greatest increases have been in those departments where the character, responsibility and nature of the work have changed. The deputy minister of justice now receives $20,000, which is up 100 per cent from what it was in 1919, whereas the deputy minister of finance is up 300 per cent.
I think it is quite correct to say that the work of the county court judge having to do with legal matters and that of the deputy minister of justice are comparable and have not changed so much in character as the work of these other deputies. I believe that is what distorts the picture and accounts for some of the points that seem to give some difficulty to the hon. member for London.
I could not admit that the county court judges in Canada have purchased the right to a larger pension at the present time because of the low salaries they have received.
I have pointed out that the salaries we provide for county court judges are provided for county court judges in all parts of Canada. I grant that in a highly industrialized province like Ontario, which I think is almost unique by reason of the provincial statute
Judges Act
setting up the county courts which prescribes a field of jurisdiction which, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Hastings-Frontenac, is almost equal in many respects to that of the superior court-I think the hon. member for London mentioned this as well- the county court judges have a heavier degree of responsibility than they have in almost any other province. It seems to me that the only one near it at all would be the province of Alberta.
That being so, it is very difficult for parliament to work out a fair salary for county court judges from one end of the country to the other and make allowance for the heavy responsibilities which are cast upon the county court judges in Ontario by provincial legislation. As I said earlier this afternoon, it seems entirely appropriate that the provincial legislature which imposes these additional duties upon county court judges should take some cognizance of having done so by allowing the county court judges some extra provincial remuneration. They have done that, and I think very properly so.
Not only have they done that, there are also a number of statutory functions which the county court judges in Ontario have to discharge and from which they receive by no means unsubstantial perquisites which add materially to their incomes. The exact amount would vary from judge to judge, and I could not give even an approximation of what they would amount to altogether. But they do receive this additional income to a greater degree than county court judges in most of the other provinces. They receive that for somewhat the same reasons that they are granted this statutory amount by the provincial government, because they have a great deal more work to do and therefore it seems only proper that they should be paid these extra amounts.
I think upon balance this practice works out reasonably well. We are glad to see that take place, because adjustments can be made in this manner, whereas it would be most difficult for the federal government to pay a higher salary to a county court judge in Ontario than to a county court judge in British Columbia, Manitoba or New Brunswick.
