speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO AGREED CHARGES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 449, to amend the Transport Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in May, 1954, Hon. W. F. A. Turgeon was appointed a commissioner under the Inquiries Act to inquire into the application and effects of agreed charges as authorized under part IV of the Transport Act taking into account (1) representations made by the province of Alberta requesting that legislation be introduced to extend the application of the one and one-third rule to the making of agreed charges, and (2) other relevant considerations including developments since the royal commission on transportation submitted its report on February 9, 1951.
The inquiry began by the holding of a meeting in Ottawa on September 13, 1954, which was attended by representatives of the interested parties. In October regional meetings were held in Winnipeg, Regina, Edmonton and Vancouver, and the final public sittings were held in Ottawa beginning on 2nd November and ending on 21st December. Thirty-nine sitting days were devoted to the inquiry.
A good deal of publicity was given to the sittings of the commission. Representations were submitted on behalf of the governments of the four western provinces, by the maritime transportation commission representing the four maritime provinces, by a number of shippers and associations representative of shippers, by the railways, by trucking associations and others.
The report of the commissioner was submitted on February 21,	1955, and was
afterwards tabled in this house. His recommendations will be found at pages 36 and 37 of the report, but are also embodied in a suggested amendment to the Transport Act which is annexed as appendix "A" of the report. The terms of this suggested amendment are embodied in the bill now before the house, which contains also one addition to which I shall refer presently and which was not specifically recommended by the commission.
A comparison of the provisions of the draft bill with those of the sections of the Transport Act which they are intended to
Transport Act
replace shows that no change is proposed in the principle of agreed charges which was accepted by this house when the Transport Act was adopted unanimously in 1938 and agreed charges were first introduced in Canada.
The principal change it is now proposed to make concerns the procedure to be followed in order that an agreed charge shall be effective. Perhaps a few words of explanation would enable hon. members to appreciate more readily the nature of the changes now to be considered.
An agreed charge, I may explain, is a charge for the transport of the whole or of a part of the goods of a shipper, negotiated or agreed upon between the shipper and one or more carriers for carriage by rail, or by rail and water. The charge is less than the normal rate because by the agreement the shipper agrees to give the carrier a stated proportion of his business between the points specified in the agreement. The parties, of course, enjoy a wide latitude in the making of the agreement and obviously its terms must afford advantages to both of them because, unless there are advantages for both of them, neither will make the agreement, being under no compulsion to do so.
To give an example, I might refer to an agreed charge made relating to the shipment in carload lots of canned goods and preserves, pickles and table sauces. This agreement obligates the shipper to deliver to the carrier for carriage for not less than 85 per cent of the shipper's traffic moving from stations in the eastern provinces to stations in Alberta and British Columbia. It will be noted that this leaves the shipper free to forward the remaining 15 per cent of his traffic into Alberta and British Columbia by other means of transport, if he so desires, and also free to forward the whole of his traffic destined to other western provinces of Canada or to stations in the eastern provinces by any means of transport that suits his convenience. I might give other examples to show that the percentage of the shipper's traffic is not invariably 85 per cent-it may be much lower-but I do wish to emphasize that the agreement is designed to meet the needs and wishes of the shipper.
An agreement having been negotiated between the parties, under existing legislation, particulars of it must be submitted to the board of transport commissioners, and notice of an application to the board for approval of the agreed charge must be given at least 30 days before the hearing, by publication in the Canada Gazette and in such other manner as the board may direct. Any shipper, or any representative body of shippers, or any

Transport Act
carrier is, after giving notice of objection, entitled to be heard in opposition to the application for approval. The board in considering the agreed charge is bound to have regard to all considerations that appear to be relevant, including the effect of the agreed charge on the net revenue of the carrier and on the business of any shipper by whom objection has been made to the charge. These formalities, which I may point out involve a delay of 30 days at the least and often much longer, having been followed, the board may approve the agreed charge which it does by issuing an order to that effect.
The commissioner, Hon. Mr. Justice Turgeon, has expressed the opinion that this procedure for bringing an agreed charge into effect should be simplified and shortened. He has recommended doing away with the requirement of the board's prior approval and allowing the agreed charge to become effective upon the expiry of a reasonable time after it has been filed with the board, and he has suggested that 20 days would be a reasonable time. This, I think it will be generally conceded, is the most important of his recommendations. In support of it I can do no better than quote the following passages to be found on pages 35 and 36 of his report. Mr. Justice Turgeon says:
X have endeavoured in the foregoing pages to describe the situation which exists today in the field of Canada's transportation economy, particular consideration being given to the position of the railways. The result of my analysis convinces me that this situation is unsatisfactory but also that it can be remedied in some measure by a reform in the practice of agreed charges, the only subject upon which I am directed to make recommendations.
Mr. Speaker, I want to emphasize particularly what next follows:
This reform must tend to enable the railways to grapple more expeditiously and therefore more efficiently with the strong and supple competition which confronts them.
In other words, the commissioner believes that the railways in making agreed charges should have much more freedom of action than they now have and be able to negotiate an agreed charge without the long delays now characteristic of our present procedure. The commissioner continues:
In my opinion the time has come to do what the royal commission on transportation refrained from doing in 1951 when conditions were very different from those which now exist and sufficient time had not gone by to test the value of what was still looked upon as a most radical and therefore potentially dangerous departure from sound methods of rate-making.
Having considered the suggestions made to me by the railways, on the one hand, for an almost perfect degree of freedom in the carrying out of their agreed charges practice, and, on the other hand, those made by others who believe that agreed charges, if allowed to continue, should be

hedged about with various degrees of restrictive regulation, I take the view that the object to be attained, as nearly as possible, is to set the railways free, but with the safeguard of certain precautions intended to preserve the rights of other interested parties.
I should now like to discuss the precautions which are contained in the present bill and are intended to preserve the rights of interested parties.
First, an agreed charge must be given publicity so that other shippers not parties to the agreement shall know what charges are to be payable on the traffic carried for their competitors.	[DOT]
Second, a reasonable delay must elapse before an agreed charge comes into effect so that during that delay other shippers who are not parties to the agreement may apply to the railway to be included in the agreement as if they were originally parties to it. The proposed bill contains a provision-and this is the addition to the commissioner's recommendations to which I referred earlier 

enabling a shipper, with the consent of the railway, to become a party to the agreement for an agreed charge merely by filing a notice of intent with the board.
Third, the proposed bill retains the provision of the existing legislation by which a shipper who considers that his business is, or will be, unjustly discriminated against by an agreed charge may at any time apply to the board for a charge to be fixed by it for the transport by the same carrier of goods of the shipper that are the same as, or similar to, and are offered for carriage under substantially similar circumstances and conditions as the goods to which the agreed charge relates.
In connection with the last two provisions I should like to say that experience has not shown that a complaint of unjust discrimination should make it necessary to cancel the agreed charge; rather it has shown that unjust discrimination can best be remedied by giving the complainant shipper a similar charge, either as a party to the agreement with the consent of the carrier, or by an order of the board fixing the charge if the carrier does not consent and the shipper meets the conditions of the statute.
Fourth, under existing legislation a shipper who considers that his business has been unjustly discriminated against as a result of the making of an agreed charge, or any representative body of shippers, can apply to the board for the withdrawal of its approval of an agreed charge only after the expiration of one year from the date of the approval of such charge by the board. The present bill provides that after an agreed

charge has been in effect for at least three months, any association or other body representative of the shippers of any locality may complain to the Minister of Transport that the agreed charge is unjustly discriminatory against it, or places its business at an unfair disadvantage; and the minister, if he is satisfied that in the public interest the complaint should be investigated, may refer it to the board for investigation.
Fifth, existing legislation permits the Minister of Transport, upon the complaint of a representative body of carriers, to refer an existing agreed charge to the board for investigation. The present bill would extend the same right to complain to any association or other body representative of the shippers of any locality, in respect of any agreed charge that has been in effect for at least three months. Where the complaint is referred to the board in this way, the board may make an order authorizing or cancelling the agreed charge complained of, or may make such other order as in the circumstances it considers proper. It has, under the new legislation, the same extensive powers as at present.
Sixth, the existing legislation does not fix the term of an agreed charge, though the board may approve it for such period as it thinks fit or without restriction of time. The present bill makes it clear that, notwithstanding anything in the agreement for an agreed charge, any party to the agreement if it has been in effect for at least one year may withdraw from it by giving 90 days' written notice.
The other changes in the act which it is proposed to effect by this bill are of minor importance and are designed to preserve the principle that agreed charges are not to be a means of competition between the railways themselves, or between the railways and regulated carriers by water.
(1)	The bill will allow a railway company incorporated in the United States and owning or operating on a railway line in Canada (a) to make agreed charges between points on its line in Canada served exclusively by it and (b) to become a party under the conditions specified in the bill to agreements for agreed charges entered into by Canadian railways. This would apply to United States railways operating wholly within the United States where they form a through route between two points in Canada.
(2)	The bill permits a carrier by water to become a party to an agreement for an agreed charge made by a railway in respect of transport from or to a competitive point or between competitive points served by the carrier by water.
Transport Act
I should like to emphasize that the principal purpose of the present bill is the simplification of the present procedure required to bring an agreed charge into effect.
In the course of the investigation by the royal commission the trucking industry took exception to the use of agreed charges by the railways and opposed any liberalization of the conditions under which they might be used. To the extent that this opposition reflects fears that the railways will thereby be enabled to eliminate highway transport, I must say that I find no basis for such theories. Even with the measure of freedom which this legislation will give to the railways, the agreed charge will still be under greater restrictions than the vast majority of highway freight rates in this country. I may say that the government is thoroughly aware of the necessity of maintaining a sound, healthy and efficient transportation industry in which each means of transport will develop according to its own particular characteristics and the demand for its services. This cannot be done, however, if the railways, and only the railways, are required to make their services available under regulations designed to meet conditions that have greatly altered or no longer obtain.
In conclusion may I say that I share the view expressed by the royal commission that it is desirable to enable the railways to grapple more expeditiously and therefore more efficiently with the strong and supple competition which confronts them. I do not ask the house to give the railways a preference over other forms of transport, but I do ask that by this bill parliament give the railways the opportunity of competing on nearly equal terms with those other forms of transport.
After the bill has received second reading, Mr. Speaker, I shall move that it be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, before which I think any representative association might appear to make representations concerning the bill.

Not only are the trucking people very much interested, but also some of the shipping companies. Hon. members will notice that the Transport Act defines "carrier" as follows:
"Carrier" means any person engaged in the transport of goods or passengers for hire or reward to whom this act applies, and includes any company that is subject to the Railway Act.
The Transport Act has never been made applicable to a large proportion of the coastal shipping of Canada. I believe it has only been proclaimed in effect in so far as shipping on the great lakes is concerned, and shipping on the St. Lawrence river and its tributaries west of the western end of the island of Orleans, and in the Mackenzie river basin. On all other waters of Canada the Transport Act does not apply. Therefore carriers engaged in business in other waters, such as those of the maritime provinces or the Pacific coast, do not come under the Transport Act and would not be considered as carriers. Therefore under the wording of the new bill they would not even have the right to appear before the board of transport commissioners to register a complaint against an agreed charge.
This brings up the question of whether this bill will interfere with the work of the royal commission which is inquiring into coastal shipping. It would appear that this commission should be able to investigate this very question of the effect of agreed charges on the shipping on our coasts. I know that some shipping firms are anxious to have representations made before the committee, and I hope they will be given that privilege.
The minister has dealt at some length with the history of agreed charges in Canada, and I do not intend to go over that history today. The authority for these charges was given in 1938 by a provision of the Transport Act which was passed in that year. This provision has been very little used until recently. In his report Hon. Mr. Turgeon pointed out on page 13 that to the end of the year 1950 -that was after the agreed charges provision had been law for 12 years-only 45 agreed charges had been made. By the end of 1954 there had been 35 additional agreed charges, making a total since 1938 of 80. It will be seen from this that the railways have taken very little advantage of this provision for agreed charges. Evidently they have now decided to move into that field on a much wider scale.
Hon. Mr. Turgeon found also that at the end of the year 1954, 6-2 per cent of the revenues of Canadian railways was earned under agreed charges, as compared with 2-4 per cent in the year 1949. This shows the increased use of these rates.

Hon. Mr. Turgeon was chairman of another commission, known as the royal commission on transportation, which reported in 1951. That commission went into this question of agreed charges but reached quite a different conclusion from the conclusion reached this year. I refer hon. members to page 95 of the earlier Turgeon report, where that commission deals with the purpose of agreed charges and points out that they should not be used to run competitors out of business. This, of course, is what the trucking industry fears. This was one of the conclusions in 1951 on the question of agreed charges:
It appears obvious that parliament did not intend the agreed charges to be a weapon to destroy or eliminate competition but rather to enable the railways to meet competition. This is clear from the reading of section 35 (1) :

. . . the board shall not approve such charge if, in its opinion, the object to be secured by the making of the agreement can, having regard to all the circumstances, adequately be secured by means of a special or competitive tariff of tolls under the Railway Act or this act.

Perhaps we will have an opportunity to say more, either in the committee or when the committee's report is received by the house.
However, I wish to say that I have taken note of the fact that the minister states he does not hold the same fear in respect of this bill that some do. The minister may take a good deal of satisfaction to himself in not holding these fears, but I would suggest that some fears have been expressed by some very responsible people and some very responsible bodies. The trucking industry of Canada has expressed some considerable fear. The mayor of the city of Calgary has expressed fear. The mayor of the city of Edmonton has expressed fear. The Alberta government, through its representatives, has expressed some fear. The automobile dealers' association has expressed fear. The representative of the Chrysler corporation in Alberta has expressed fear.
I am not going to pit the wisdom of the minister against the wisdom of the representatives of these organizations. I would say that these organizations are composed of very responsible men, and for the most part men who have had some practical experience in shipping. They do express some fear in respect of this matter. The trucking industry of Canada, for instance, in a press dispatch appearing in the Montreal Gazette the other day, said:
William C. Norris of Montreal, president of the trucking associations, said the truckers are not fighting the proposed streamlined procedure for making agreed charges. However, they wanted the same right as water carriers to protest contracts they believed to be discriminatory.

Transport Act
The mayor of the city of Calgary-I am reading from a press dispatch in the Calgary Herald; I am sorry I have not the date, but it was when the transport commission was sitting in Edmonton-said:
The recent development of agreed charges between the railways and some eastern Canadian shippers "reflects anything but credit to those associated with it". Mayor D. H. Mackay said in Edmonton Thursday when he submitted a brief on behalf of the city to the royal commission on agreed charges.
Mayor Mackay went on to say:
The principle of agreed charges should "find itself completely and without reservation" included in the one and one-third rule, the mayor said. He added that the railways' "new wrinkle" was a "wilful disregard of the intent of principle".
That is pretty strong language. The mayor also said:
"We cannot continue to favour one section of the country at the expense of the other, and excuse ourselves on the theory that western provinces must be sacrificed upon the altar of competition that may exist on the coastal waterfronts of this country."

speechtext: If the hon. member is quoting press reports concerning matters which are not before the house, it is not relevant, and therefore it should not be read. subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO AGREED CHARGES
speechtext:
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, if I did not read that rule correctly. However, I will say that the mayor of Edmonton expressed himself before the commission in a similar way to the mayor of the city of Calgary. The automobile dealers' association has claimed that this will seriously affect the price of automobiles, to the detriment of

their sales or to the detriment of the consumer. The trucking industry has even declared that this will perhaps mean the end of the trucking of automobiles on the main highways from the manufacturers to the retailers.
I should like to read further, but according to your ruling I evidently cannot do it. I shall have to think that ruling over a little further, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO AGREED CHARGES
speechtext:
I shall read citation 265. It is not invoked very often. I can tell the hon. member that latitude is too often given to hon. members to violate this rule during debate. I must remind hon. members from time to time that the rule exists. The citation reads:
It is not in order to read articles in newspapers, letters or communications emanating from persons outside the house and referring to, or commenting on, or denying anything said by a member or expressing any opinion reflecting on proceedings within the house.
The discussion of the second reading of a bill is a proceeding in the house.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO AGREED CHARGES
speechtext:
I shall not debate the point of order, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps it is because of the latitude that has been given that the seriousness of the point was not indelibly impressed upon my mind. It is nearly six o'clock, and I shall not detain the house beyond another half minute.
We have all received telegrams and requests from various organizations asking that the bill be sent to the committee. Perhaps it was not the intention to send the bill to the committee. If the concession is granted by the minister, then we wish to thank him very much. I am sure the organizations concerned will appreciate that concession, if it can be called one, and we shall deal further with the matter either before the committee or when it comes back to the house.
